**Reasoning.** I dug into how Codex resolves the realtime endpoints and couldn't definitively pin down whether `experimental_realtime_ws_base_url` defaults to something derived from `openai_base_url` or to an independent host. But that unknown turns out not to matter, because this PR is correct either way:

| | #25 (this PR) | #27 |
|---|---|---|
| WS default is independent | works | works |
| WS default derives from `openai_base_url` | works — pinned off the router | breaks — WS leg still hits `server.on("upgrade")` → `426` |

#27 only adds an HTTP `POST /live` route; it never touches the upgrade handler. This PR pins **both** realtime base URLs, so it covers both cases. It dominates, so it wins.

Two things I confirmed against Codex 0.145.0 while checking:

- `experimental_realtime_ws_base_url` and `experimental_realtime_webrtc_call_base_url` are both real root keys in `ConfigToml` — this isn't relying on anything invented.
- There's also a `[realtime] transport` key with `webrtc` and `websocket` variants. If those are alternatives rather than simultaneous legs, a user on `transport = "websocket"` is precisely the case #27 could not have served.

**One follow-up, not a blocker.** This hardcodes `https://api.openai.com/v1` as the WS base. I couldn't confirm from the Codex binary that this matches Codex's own default when the key is unset — if it doesn't, we'd be pinning a host that's correct-by-accident. Could you share where that value came from? If it's from Codex docs or source, a comment citing it would be worth adding. If it was inferred, worth an issue to verify against a live Voice session.

The `rootHasValue` guard preserving user-owned endpoints and the byte-for-byte `disable` restore test are what made this easy to trust. Thanks for the care on those.

Closing this in favor of #25, which has now merged. Want to be clear that this is **not** a code-quality call — the implementation here is genuinely good, and I'd rather explain properly than close it silently.

**Why #25 instead.** Both PRs fix "Voice Mode breaks when the router is enabled," but with opposite designs: #25 keeps voice traffic *out* of the router via config overrides, this one routes it *through*. I couldn't definitively determine whether `experimental_realtime_ws_base_url` defaults to a host derived from `openai_base_url` or an independent one. That unknown decided it:

| | #25 | #27 (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| WS default is independent | works | works |
| WS default derives from `openai_base_url` | works | **breaks** |

This PR adds `handleNativeLive` for `POST /live` and `/v1/live`, but doesn't touch `server.on("upgrade")` in `src/router.mjs`, which still answers `426 Upgrade Required`. So if the realtime WebSocket leg follows `openai_base_url`, it would still land on the router and get rejected — voice fixed on the call leg, still broken on the socket leg. #25 pins both URLs and is correct in either case.

One more thing that pushed it: Codex 0.145.0 has a `[realtime] transport` key with `webrtc` and `websocket` variants. If those are alternatives rather than simultaneous legs, anyone on `transport = "websocket"` was never served by this approach.

**What was good here, sincerely:** the header allowlist in `nativeLiveHeaders`, the browser-origin rejection, the abort wiring on both `request.aborted` and `response.close`, and especially the test asserting Kimi routing stays untouched. That last one is the kind of test most people skip.

**If you want to revisit this:** the passthrough approach has a real advantage #25 lacks — voice shows up in router activity tracking (`setRoute` with `model: "voice"`), where #25 makes it invisible. If you're up for a follow-up that also proxies the WebSocket upgrade rather than 426-ing it, that would be a strictly better end state than where we are now, and I'd review it seriously.

Also worth knowing: the red `test (windows-latest)` on this PR was never your fault — `alias reads pick up rewritten state and reverse lookups resolve` is flaky on `main` independently. Sorry that sat on your PR looking like a failure.

Closing this in favor of #31.

After deploying, this change caused a regression on the Kimi OAuth path: `litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - text content is empty. Received Model Group=kimi-oauth-k3`.

Root cause of the regression: `kimi-oauth-k3` is routed through `oauth-forwarder.mjs`, whose `foldInterveningAssistantMessages` already folds (and splices out) intervening assistant messages — including empty-content ones — that sit between a tool-call assistant and its tool results. It can only do that when the tool-call assistant and tool results are present in the messages. By stripping `function_call` / `function_call_output` items from the compaction input in `summarize()`, this PR removed exactly the anchors that `foldInterveningAssistantMessages` needs, so empty-content assistant messages from the history were no longer folded out and reached Kimi, which rejects them with "text content is empty". Confirmed by the router log: zero `text content is empty` errors before this change, the first one immediately after.

This PR is also redundant: #31 (coalescing consecutive assistant messages in `api-forwarder`) already fixes the `tool call result does not follow tool call (2013)` compaction failure for `openai-compatible` providers (MiniMax, DeepSeek, Qwen, etc.), because the compaction request flows router → LiteLLM → `api-forwarder`, where the coalesce runs. The Kimi OAuth path was already handled by `foldInterveningAssistantMessages` before this PR.

Reverting. The minimax compaction 2013 stays fixed via #31.

Update: this PR also covers the routed **compaction** path for openai-compatible providers (MiniMax, DeepSeek, Qwen, etc.), because the compaction request flows router → LiteLLM → `api-forwarder`, where this coalesce runs — so it fixes the `tool call result does not follow tool call (2013)` compaction failure without needing to strip tool items.

A companion PR (#32) that stripped tool-call items from the compaction input was tried and **reverted**: it defeated `oauth-forwarder`'s existing `foldInterveningAssistantMessages`, which needs the tool-call assistant + tool results present to fold out empty-content intervening assistant messages, and that produced a new `text content is empty` regression on `kimi-oauth-k3`. The Kimi OAuth path was already handled by that fold; this PR handles the openai-compatible paths. See #32 for the details.

One correction worth recording. The report notes that `catalog.execCodex()` already handles this with `shell: true`. That code doesn't exist in this repo — `grep -rn "shell: true" src/*.mjs` returns nothing, and there is no `execCodex`. So `captureNative()` had the identical defect, and the bug was slightly broader than described.

The more damaging half was the bare `catch`. A spawn failure and a signed-out session were indistinguishable, so an unrunnable binary read as "logged out" and `buildMergedCatalog` dropped every native model with nothing surfaced. Picking the right shim alone would have fixed your case while leaving that silent-failure class intact.

What changed:

- `findCodexBinary()` prefers `.exe`/`.com`/`.cmd`/`.bat` over an extensionless PATH entry on Windows, instead of trusting `where.exe` ordering
- `.cmd`/`.bat` run through a shell with the path quoted, since Codex is routinely installed under a directory containing spaces
- `codexAuthStatus()` separates `probe-failed` from `signed-out`
- the catalog build now refuses to run on `probe-failed` rather than emptying the picker
- `bin/doctor` reports the probe failure as its own check

Tests cover the exact `where.exe` output from your report, with the platform injectable so Windows behaviour is verified from any host. CI passes on `test (windows-latest)` and `desktop (windows-latest)`.

I don't have a Windows machine, so the shim selection and quoting are verified by unit test rather than on real hardware. If you can confirm on your setup I'd appreciate it — reopen if anything still misbehaves.

`src/config-manager.mjs` pins both realtime endpoints away from the router so Voice never inherits the Responses-only base URL:

```toml
experimental_realtime_webrtc_call_base_url = "https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex"
experimental_realtime_ws_base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1"
```

Worth checking your `~/.codex/config.toml` for those two keys. If they're missing, update and re-run the installer or `./bin/doctor --fix`. They're only written when you don't already have your own values, so a pre-existing override is preserved.

Closing on that basis, but I'm not certain it's your case — I don't know which version you were running. **If those keys are present and Voice still fails, please reopen with your `codex-router` version and commit.** That would mean a second cause, and I'd want to see it.

Your architectural point is separate and still stands: routing a native model back to OpenAI doesn't make the router transparent to every OpenAI feature. The router does terminate all Codex traffic and rejects upgrades with `426` (`src/router.mjs:818`), so Voice is patched endpoint-by-endpoint rather than structurally. The next native feature on an unsupported transport would break the same way.

Making native parent-agent traffic bypass the router entirely is a real design change, not a bug fix — it would need Codex to support per-provider base URLs so only external subagents point at the loopback. If you'd like that tracked, open a separate issue for it and it won't get lost behind the Voice symptom.

Thanks — models.dev is a good pointer, and the maintenance argument for it is fair.

Some context on where the gap actually is. `bin/curate-models` already queries each provider's own `/v1/models` endpoint live (`src/model-discovery.mjs`), lists whatever isn't in the checked-in registry, and lets you toggle entries into protected local state. So *discovery* is covered, with first-party provenance.

What discovery can't supply is the metadata the router needs to route well: context window, auto-compact threshold, reasoning levels, input modalities. Curated models currently get conservative defaults for those. That's the real gap models.dev would fill, and pricing on top.

The tradeoff worth being explicit about: that metadata drives routing behaviour, so sourcing it from a community aggregator rather than the provider means a network dependency at catalog build time and a new supply-chain surface for values that decide how requests are shaped. Not disqualifying — the registry is hand-maintained today, which has its own staleness problem — but it's a different trust model than "the provider told us".

A plausible middle path: keep `/v1/models` as the source of truth for *which* models exist, and use models.dev only to fill metadata defaults for curated entries, with whatever it returns being overridable locally.

Leaving this open as a proposal rather than closing it. No commitment yet, but it's a real gap and the suggestion is on point.

Thanks for the PR — the hash-verified lock infrastructure (`requirements/litellm.lock` + `--require-hashes` installers + the regression test) is a genuinely nice hardening pattern, and you clearly hit a real install problem. That said, we're not going to merge this as-is. A few reasons:

**The stated root cause is inaccurate.** `litellm==1.93.0` *is* published on PyPI and is not yanked. What's actually true is that 1.93.0 only ships `manylinux` wheels plus an sdist — no macOS or Windows wheels — so on those platforms pip falls back to a source build, which fails without a build toolchain. That's presumably the failure you hit (Windows?). We verified a clean `uv pip install 'litellm[proxy]==1.93.0'` succeeds on macOS.

**Downgrading is the wrong direction.** Pinning 1.83.9 rolls the gateway back ~4 months and ~10 minor versions on the component that processes prompts, credentials, and tool calls. litellm 1.94.1 and 1.95.0 both ship macOS and Windows wheels, so bumping forward solves the same platform problem without reverting any fixes.

**Unrelated changes are bundled in.** The first commit switches DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro to the Responses API and introduces a per-model `protocol` override across the forwarder, registry, and LiteLLM config. That's a behavioral routing change that needs its own PR with evidence that DeepSeek's API actually serves `/responses`.

If you'd like to resubmit: regenerate the lock against 1.95.0 (or latest stable with full platform wheel coverage), correct the root-cause description, and split the DeepSeek change into a separate PR. The lock-file approach itself would be welcome.

Thanks for the suggestion — a tap is something I'd like to do, with one caveat on the approach.

A self-contained Bun/Deno executable unfortunately isn't possible today: the router is Node on the front, but at runtime it launches a Python LiteLLM gateway from a pinned virtualenv (`litellm[proxy]==1.95.0`). A compiled JS binary can't carry the Python side, so single-file distribution is off the table unless the LiteLLM dependency is replaced entirely.

A regular Homebrew formula in a tap is doable, though:

- `brew install` would put the app in `libexec` with the Python deps built from pinned resources
- upgrades would go through `brew upgrade` instead of the built-in `codex-router update` (which assumes a git checkout)
- you'd still run `codex-router setup` once after install for Codex integration and provider keys, since that part is interactive

The main prerequisite is cutting versioned releases, which the repo doesn't have yet.

Question for you: would a tap that still requires the one-time `setup` step cover your use case, or were you specifically after a zero-config single binary? That determines whether this is a packaging task or a much bigger architectural one.

One more piece of architecture context that I think changes the calculus here.

codex-router isn't a CLI you invoke. Installation registers a background service — a LaunchAgent on macOS (`RunAtLoad` + `KeepAlive`), a systemd unit on Linux (`Restart=always`) — that comes up at login and stays up. After setup you just run `codex` and routing happens transparently. You never type a router command again except for occasional maintenance like `doctor` or adding a provider.

That's why the single-binary angle doesn't buy much here even setting the Python dependency aside. You'd download one file, it would immediately tell you to run the interactive setup, and then you'd never invoke it again because the daemon is doing the work. Self-contained executables are a real win for tools you run constantly (ripgrep, fd, that shape of thing) — for a background service, it's mostly cosmetic.

What I do think is legitimate in your request has nothing to do with binaries: package managers *manage* things. `brew upgrade`, `brew uninstall`, knowing what's actually on your machine, and not piping curl into sh — which plenty of developers and most corporate environments simply won't do. That's the real gap, and it's the part worth serving.

So the earlier question still decides the scope: is a tap that still needs the one-time `codex-router setup` useful to you? If yes, this is a packaging task and I'll look at cutting releases. If what you actually want is zero-config, that's a much larger architectural change and I'd rather be upfront that it isn't near-term.

Thanks for the report — root cause found and fixed in #60.

Codex's effort picker parses reasoning levels into a fixed enum and silently drops values it doesn't recognize. The `max` tier we added to several models in #54 only became a valid value in **Codex 0.143.0**, so on earlier builds it vanishes from the menu — that's why GLM-5.2 shows a lone High (it declares high + max) and DeepSeek V4 Flash shows Light/High instead of three tiers (it declares low + high + max).

Two things will get your third effort back:

1. **Upgrade Codex to 0.143 or newer** — the Max tier then appears natively (this is also why it already works on some setups).
2. **Update the router** — it now detects your installed Codex version and, on pre-0.143 builds, republishes the max tier as XHigh so it stays selectable. Either way it routes upstream at maximum effort; only the label differs.

Note the picker was never sending less reasoning than intended — requests still routed at the model's full default tier upstream. This was a picker display/selection issue only.

The tap should would still be useful. One time setup is still fine because the tap is more about having centralized source of updates. Switching from litellm to a similar provider with a JS api could solve the original problem though.

Rebasing would have meant re-authoring the model definitions into the new per-file layout anyway, and there were a couple of changes worth making to the runtime pieces along the way. Details below so nothing is lost.

### Landed as-is

- **Stripping `client_metadata` from forwarded payloads.** The most valuable part of this PR, and not Gemini-specific — `main` had no handling for it anywhere. Applied to the API forwarder, the Kimi OAuth forwarder, and the routed `/responses` path as you had it, plus `summarize()` in `router.mjs`, which also spreads the caller payload into the gateway request and was leaking the field on the compaction path.
- **Dropping `web_search_options` for Gemini.**
- **`-EncodedCommand` for the Windows hidden key prompt.**
- **The `legacy-migration.mjs` regex escape.** Worth flagging how much this one mattered. The pattern is built in a template literal, so `\s` collapsed to a literal `s` and the compiled regex was `^s*key s*=s*...` — it matched only unindented keys with no spacing around `=`. So `model_catalog_json = "..."`, the conventional TOML spacing, was invisible to `detectLegacyInstallations()`. That left `unknownConflict` false for a foreign router's catalog, which is exactly what clears migration to run over an installation the router does not own. Good catch; it has a test now covering five spacing variants.

### Changed

**`ensureGeminiThoughtSignatures` set the sentinel unconditionally.** A real signature Gemini had already returned got overwritten with `skip_thought_signature_validator`, so the model lost the reasoning it was being asked to continue from. It now fills only where a signature is absent, with a regression test that fails against the unconditional version.

**Provider detection collapsed into one `isGeminiProvider()` predicate.** Dropped the `id.includes("gemini")` substring check — it would also match a non-Google provider that happened to have "gemini" in its id.

**The PowerShell candidate loop now keeps the first non-ENOENT failure rather than the last error.** That is what produced the `spawnSync pwsh.exe ENOENT` in the reported trace: `powershell.exe` had already failed for some real reason, then `pwsh.exe` — absent on a stock Windows box — overwrote it. The underlying error was never visible to anyone.

### Not landed

The curated Gemini model definitions. `gemini-api` is a catalog-only provider by design (see `AGENTS.md`): it ships no preselected models, and users curate with `bin/curate-models gemini-api` after storing a key. Preloading them reverses that policy, so it deserves its own discussion rather than riding along with a bug fix.

Two things your report turned up that were larger than the original bug:

**The failure was self-perpetuating.** The installer records the current revision, fast-forwards the checkout, runs setup, and restores the old revision on any non-zero exit. So the fix for a setup-path bug was fetched and then discarded by the rollback, and every retry reproduced the same failure. Setup now exits 2 for "the checkout is healthy, configuration is unfinished" — a declined prompt, a missing credential, a bad argument — and both installers keep the update. Any other non-zero exit still rolls back. Credential entry is also best-effort in guided runs now, so a broken key prompt warns and finishes the install instead of taking it down.

**The `\s` escape was a safety bug, not a cosmetic one.** Built in a template literal, the pattern compiled to `^s*key s*=s*...`, matching only unindented keys with no spacing around `=`. So `model_catalog_json = "..."` — the conventional TOML form — was invisible to `detectLegacyInstallations()`, which left `unknownConflict` false for a foreign router's catalog and cleared migration to run over an installation the router does not own. Covered by a test across five spacing variants.

**On the Gemini models.** Preloading them is still not something we want — `gemini-api` is catalog-only by design and users curate with `bin/curate-models gemini-api`. But you were solving a real problem: storing a key printed "The provider is enabled" and told you to reopen the picker, which was empty, with nothing anywhere saying curation was the next step. That is now fixed — storing a key for a provider with no registered models names the exact command to run next. The discoverability gap you hit was real even though the fix landed differently.

Reviewed in depth. The security architecture is sound — I want to say that first, because the rest of this is a list of problems and it would give the wrong impression otherwise.

**What holds up.** Credential isolation is clean: `nativeHeaders()` copies only the fixed `FORWARD_HEADERS` allowlist and is only ever sent to the hardcoded `NATIVE_BASE`, never to a user-controlled destination. The fail-closed path is real — the `engine.native` branch in `describeRequest()` throws and returns before the gateway and local branches, so there is no path where a missing session falls back to the gateway with a native slug. No credential, header, or transcript reaches a log; upstream error bodies are never echoed. Effort clamping is correct in both directions and properly tested. 497 tests, 492 pass, 0 fail.

Three things to fix, then the policy question.

---

**1. Mid-stream errors are silently swallowed and returned as a complete transcript.** This is the one I'd most want fixed.

`streamedResponseText()` recognizes only `response.output_text.delta` and "anything with a `.response` field". It has no concept of stream failure. Reproduced directly:

- Deltas followed by `{"type":"error","error":{"message":"upstream overloaded"}}` → returns the partial text, error dropped.
- Deltas followed by a proper `{"type":"response.failed","response":{"status":"failed",...}}` → `deltas.join()` is non-empty, so the failed status is never inspected at all.

A backend error partway through generation produces a plausible-looking truncated transcript with zero indication anything went wrong. That cuts against the vision-bridge's own "evidence, not impressions" rule in AGENTS.md — a downstream model quotes it as if it were the whole image. The existing `unreadableBlock()` degradation path is the correct behavior here and it never fires. Suggest treating a `response.failed`/`error` event, or a completed `response` whose `status !== "completed"`, as a thrown error.

**2. Request-time resolution skips the auth gate that the other two call sites apply.** The candidate criteria are enforced in three independently-maintained places, and they disagree:

- `src/catalog.mjs:531` gates on `openaiAuthenticated && !loginFree`.
- `src/control.mjs` `shippedNativeVisionEngines()` gates via merged-catalog membership — equivalent.
- `src/router.mjs:726` (`bridgeVisionInput`, the actual request-time path) reads `NATIVE_CATALOG_PATH` directly with **no auth check**.

That file can legitimately be stale — `nativeCatalog()` explicitly reuses a cached on-disk capture when a fresh probe fails, and nothing forces a refresh before the router reads it. So: operator signs out, `catalog.mjs` correctly stops advertising the engine, but the pinned setting still points at it, and every bridged paste on every text-only routed model attempts a native call against the stale capture. It fails, and there is no fallback to another candidate within that resolution — the image degrades to "unreadable" rather than quietly using a still-valid paid or local engine. Best fix is one shared helper rather than three hand-maintained candidate builders.

**3. Evidence cache isn't partitioned by account.** `evidenceCache` keys on `slug + effort + url` with no session identifier. That was fine when the paying credential was always the router's own install-scoped one. Now that a native call is authorized by the caller's live session, a cache hit skips any re-check that the current session is entitled to that model. Not a confidentiality leak — you need the identical image bytes to get a hit — but it is an entitlement bypass on the hit path. Keying native engines on `chatgpt-account-id` from `FORWARD_HEADERS` would close it. Lower severity than the two above.

---

**On the AGENTS.md question you raised.** You were right to flag it rather than merge quietly. My read is that this violates the rule as written. The rule names exactly one exception:

> A registry engine's call goes through the same gateway, credential, and request profile as any other routed turn. Do not add a second upstream path, a separate vision API key, or an external CLI dependency for a hosted engine. The one sanctioned exception is the local engine (`vision-bridge local`)...

Your code comment says it too — "Two call shapes" becomes "Three call shapes," and the third is a hosted engine that bypasses the gateway for `NATIVE_BASE` directly.

Your intent argument isn't frivolous: no stored credential, no CLI, no new install step. But two things cut against it. The rule enumerates a single named exception whose justification ("no credential to store") is structurally the same as yours — if a general "no new credential" test were intended, that's what would have been written. And the native path skips the scaffolding the provider checklist requires elsewhere in the same file: no `doctor` reachability check, and no usage/limits surfacing, which matters concretely here because ChatGPT-plan quota spent transcribing images becomes invisible spend.

Your report turned out not to be an image bug at all — the image fix you were after was already on main. What blocked you was the updater: `requireManagedCheckout()` treated any output from `git status --porcelain` as local changes, and that includes **untracked** files. One stray file in the checkout from an editor or an antivirus scan, and every future update was refused with no way past it and no indication which file was responsible.

#102 fixes that: only tracked edits hold an update now, the error names the specific files, and `--force` gets past them. A fast-forward never replaces an untracked file anyway — git refuses that collision itself with a precise message — so counting untracked files only ever stranded people.

**But merging it does not unstick you**, because the broken code is the updater itself. You need one manual step first. In PowerShell:


Root-caused. There are **two different problems** in this report, and the one in the title is not a router bug.

## The 503 is OpenAI's edge, relayed faithfully

The Envoy-shaped sentence — "upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: remote connection failure" — appears nowhere in this codebase. Grepping `src/`, `test/`, and `docs/` for `upstream connect`, `reset reason`, and `before headers` returns no matches. The router does not synthesize it.

The local URL in the message is a red herring. Codex's own error template is:

```
unexpected status <status>: <body>, url: <url>, cf-ray: <...>, auth error: <...>
```

So `, url: http://127.0.0.1:4102/...` is **Codex naming the endpoint it dialed**, appended after the body. The Envoy sentence is the *body* Codex received. The router relays native non-2xx untouched — the error-translation branch at `src/router.mjs:1131` is gated on `route &&`, and native traffic has `route === undefined`, so it falls through to `pipeResponse`, which copies the upstream status and body byte-for-byte.

Corroborating: a live install's usage log recorded upstream `520` responses alongside the 503s. `520` is a **Cloudflare-only** status code — it can only have originated at chatgpt.com.

"Especially GPT-5.6 Luna" is a volume artifact. Normalized by request count, the 503 rate is essentially identical across the native GPT models (well under 0.1% each), and one of them recorded none at all. It looks model-specific because Luna gets the most traffic. It is native-only because only native traffic goes to chatgpt.com; routed traffic goes to LiteLLM.

`Reconnecting /5` is Codex's own retry loop reacting to a 5xx.

**So for the 503 itself there is nothing to fix here.** The actionable ask would be retry/backoff behavior, not routing.

## `error decoding response body` IS a router defect

This one is real, and it is a fidelity bug rather than the origin of the failure.

`pipeResponse` uses `.pipe()` (`src/http-utils.mjs:98-100`), which does not forward errors or propagate `destroy()`. When an upstream SSE body errors mid-stream, the response is left half-written and never ended. The promise rejects, `handleResponses` rethrows, and the top-level handler does `response.destroy()` (`src/router.mjs:1337-1338`). On an in-flight chunked body that emits an RST *without* the terminating `0\r\n\r\n` — which reqwest reports as exactly `network error: error decoding response body`.

So an upstream hiccup that should surface as a clean error instead surfaces as a corrupt stream. Reproduced against the real `pipeResponse`, both for a transform throwing in `_flush` and for an upstream body error.

Contributing factor: nothing configures undici, so Node's default `bodyTimeout` of 300s applies. A gap of over five minutes between SSE chunks on a long reasoning turn errors the body — and the router then converts that into a socket reset instead of a graceful close.

## Your aside about the health endpoint was the most valuable part of this report

You mentioned almost in passing that `status` showed the service loaded/running while the health endpoint was unavailable. That is a **separate, serious, reproducible bug**, and I would not have gone looking for it otherwise.

`readProviderSelection()` (`src/provider-selection.mjs:76-95`) is the only state reader in the router's hot path that throws instead of degrading — `readNativeAliases`, `readNativeRedirect`, and `catalogModels` all swallow. It throws `Unknown provider: X` for any id not in the `PROVIDERS` map, and that map is built at module import, so it is frozen for the life of the process.

It is called from the **first statement** of `healthPayload()` (`src/router.mjs:367`, before the gateway probe at `:376`) and from every `/responses` turn (`:1020`, `:1024`).

So a single selection file naming an id the *running* build doesn't know — version skew after an update, a CLI invoked from a newer checkout, a renamed or removed provider — makes **every** request 502 and the health endpoint fail, until the service is restarted. The process stays alive and bound the whole time, which is why the supervisor reports it as healthy.

Reproduced offline, no upstream contacted:

```
[unauth /health]            HTTP 502  {"error":{"type":"local_router_error",...}}
[caller POST /v1/responses] HTTP 502  {"error":{"type":"local_router_error",...}}
--- process still alive? --- true
```

A second, benign contributor to the same observation: launchd supervises `src/start.mjs`, not the router, and the router starts last behind a 300s LiteLLM gate, so `status` legitimately reports running while port 4102 is unbound for up to ~390s after logon.

Fixes for both defects are in progress.

## What would confirm which one hit you

Run this right after a failure:

```bash
python3 -c "
import json
for l in open('$HOME/.codex/codex-router/usage-events.jsonl'):
    e=json.loads(l)
    if e.get('provider')=='openai' and e.get('status')!=200: print(e)
" | tail -20
grep -c 'request failed' ~/.codex/codex-router/router.log
```

- **No** matching event plus a rising `request failed` count → the turn died inside the router. Then compare `cat ~/.codex/codex-router/enabled-providers.json` against the providers your running build knows, and a mismatch confirms the wedge.

One reason this was hard to diagnose at all: `src/router.mjs:1329` logs the bare string `[codex-router] request failed` and never logs the error object, and the LaunchAgent hard-sets `CODEX_ROUTER_QUIET=1`, which suppresses the per-request status line. On a production install the log ends up carrying almost no information about actual requests. That is being fixed alongside the rest.

Not your fault, and it's a real bug. The cause isn't compaction — it's token accounting upstream of it.

## What's happening

Codex decides when to auto-compact by reading `input_tokens` from each `response.completed`. opencode's Go endpoint stopped reporting prompt tokens for its **DeepSeek V4** models around 2026-08-06. Codex's context counter therefore never climbs, never crosses the 900,000-token threshold the router advertises, and never fires compaction — until the provider itself rejects the request at its real limit.

Reproduced from a live install's own logs:

```
litellm.ContextWindowExceededError: ... Error from provider (Console Go): [invalid_request_error]
This model's maximum context length is 1048576 tokens. However, you requested 1050034 tokens
model=opencode-go-deepseek-v4-flash
```

One ordinary turn carrying 1,050,034 tokens — 150K past the point where compaction should have run. Same symptom you described.

**It's the provider's endpoint, not the router.** On the same install, same days, same LiteLLM path, same forwarder:

- `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash` — ~91% of successful responses report `input_tokens: 0`
- `opencode-go/kimi-k3` — 52 of 52 report correctly
- `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` via the **direct** DeepSeek API — all correct

And it's dated. Traffic on 2026-08-05 reported tokens correctly; from 08-06 onward it's almost entirely zeros. So this is specific to opencode's Go endpoint for the DeepSeek V4 family, not to LiteLLM, `stream_options`, or codex-router's request handling.

**`/goal` isn't special.** Goal mode has no router-side compaction handling at all. It's just the workload that accumulates a million tokens fastest, which is why you hit this there rather than in ordinary use. Your instinct to mention it was a good one — it's what made the volume high enough to expose the accounting bug.

Also ruled out: the advertised context window is **correct**, not inflated. The router advertises 1,048,576, and the provider's own error confirms that is its real maximum. That was my leading hypothesis and the evidence killed it.

## Would you confirm it's the same on your machine?

One line, PowerShell:

```powershell
node -e "const fs=require('fs'),p=process.env.USERPROFILE+'\\.codex\\codex-router\\usage-events.jsonl';const ev=fs.readFileSync(p,'utf8').split('\n').filter(Boolean).map(l=>{try{return JSON.parse(l)}catch{return null}}).filter(e=>e&&e.model==='opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash'&&e.status===200);console.log('responses:',ev.length,'| zero-input:',ev.filter(e=>e.inputTokens===0).length,'| max-input:',Math.max(0,...ev.map(e=>e.inputTokens||0)))"
```

A high `zero-input` count confirms it. Also useful: did Codex's `/status` context bar sit near empty during that session? That's the user-visible fingerprint — the bar looks fine right up until the provider rejects the turn.

## What's being fixed here

The upstream regression is opencode's to fix, but two router-side defects this exposed are ours:

1. **Routed compaction is invisible.** `handleRoutedCompaction` returns before the metering and logging every other path performs, so a routed compaction — success *or* failure — produces no usage event and no log line. There is currently no way to answer "was compaction even attempted?" from the router's own telemetry. That's why this took real digging.
2. **Compaction doesn't resolve subagent payloads.** Routed turns resolve `agent_message` handoffs into readable text; the compaction path doesn't, so a compaction inside a `/goal` or subagent session ships opaque payloads to the model. AGENTS.md requires the same handling on both endpoints. Unrelated to your token problem, but it lives in exactly the `/goal` + routed-model intersection you were in.

A third possible mitigation — having the router substitute an estimated token count when the upstream reports zero — would paper over the provider bug, but it's a heuristic that risks compacting too early. Not shipping that without a live test.

Worth also reporting the zero-token responses to opencode, since only they can actually fix the source.

Independent review found a HIGH defect in this PR's own mechanism. Fixed and pushed as a second commit.

**The bug.** `endStreamedResponse` wrote its terminal frame assuming the previous write ended on a line boundary. That only holds when upstream fails cleanly *between* two events. A real reset lands wherever it lands, and transforms forward upstream's chunk boundaries verbatim, so the client is usually holding an unterminated `data:` line — a single `output_text.delta` can carry a long span. Reproduced on the wire:

```
data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","delta":"partial-chunk-no-newlineevent: error
data: {"type":"error","code":"local_router_stream_failed",...}
```

With no newline before it, a conforming parser reads `event: error` as *more of the previous event's data*. So the one signal saying the router lost the stream is never recognized as an error, becomes garbage appended to the last delta, and a lenient consumer can render it as model output. That is the silent corruption this function exists to prevent — the PR was defeating its own purpose in the common case.

The existing tests never caught it because `failingSseUpstream()` always writes a complete `data: first\n\n` before erroring, exercising only the lucky path.

**The fix.** Prefix the frame with a blank line so it always begins a fresh event regardless of where upstream died. Inert when the stream did end cleanly — a blank line with no buffered fields dispatches nothing.

New test asserts the field name begins its own line, that a real SSE parse over the blank-line dispatch boundary finds an event declaring `event: error` with parseable data carrying `local_router_stream_failed`, and that `unterminatedevent` never appears. Verified RED against the unfixed code (fails with "the terminal frame was glued onto the unterminated data line") and GREEN with the fix.

Two updates: the highest-risk unverified item is now proven on CI, and a regression this PR introduced is fixed.

## The exit-code chain is executed now, not reasoned about

The thing actually blocking this was item 2 — whether `WScript.Quit status` propagates the wrapper's exit code. If it doesn't, Task Scheduler sees success on every crash and the restart policy silently dies, trading a console window for an availability bug.

That doesn't need a registered task to test. It needs `wscript.exe`, which `windows-latest` runners have. There's now a Windows-only test that generates the launcher through this PR's own `render-launcher` command, writes the exact BOM + UTF-16LE bytes `writeLaunchers()` produces, and executes it under both `cscript.exe` and `wscript.exe //B //NoLogo`:

- a wrapper exiting **42** must reach the host as **42**
- a wrapper exiting **0** must stay **0** — a clean shutdown reported as failure would have the task restart a router the user deliberately stopped
- a wrapper that **never ran** must not report success

It passed on CI:

```
✔ the generated Windows launcher returns the wrapper's exit code to its script host (1440.281ms)
```

**What that closes, precisely:** item 3 (wscript accepts the UTF-16LE-with-BOM file — a parse failure would be immediate red), and the half of item 2 that is a property of this code. It also incidentally proves the `Chr(34)` quoting survives a state dir containing a space.

**What it does not close, and I don't want to imply otherwise:** whether Task Scheduler *interprets* a non-zero action exit as a task failure and re-triggers `RestartCount`/`RestartInterval`. That is scheduler policy and needs a real registered task. Items 1 (console window actually hidden), 4 (`schtasks /Create /TR` fallback), 6 (upgrade against a prior install) and 7 (non-ASCII `%LOCALAPPDATA%`) also still need a real machine.

The `Err.Number <> 0` guard is likewise still unexecuted — it turns out not to be reachable on a normal host, since the Run command is hardcoded to `cmd.exe` and `CreateProcess` resolves that from the system directory regardless of PATH. It stays as belt-and-braces.

## A regression this PR introduced, now fixed

`endTask()` ran before `installTask()`, so in a restricted or non-elevated shell the registration throws, the catch swallows it, `/Run` is skipped — **and the previously-running instance had already been killed**. Pre-PR, a failed install left the old router running. That is strictly worse than what it replaced.

The order is kept, because `-Force` re-registration can orphan Task Scheduler's tracking of a live instance and make a later `/End` a no-op against a real process. The failure path recovers instead, and it queries before acting: by that point both registration routes have failed, so the surviving state is either the previous definition or nothing at all, and the code cannot know which. A bare `/Run` against a name that is gone recovers nothing and reports its own error over the one that matters.

Restoring the old definition was considered and rejected — nothing is snapshotted to restore *from*, and re-creating it means re-creating the console-visible `cmd.exe` action this launcher exists to remove.

Three smaller ones alongside it:

- `writeLaunchers()` moved inside the `try`, so a `renameSync` over a `.vbs` held open by a running `wscript.exe` can no longer throw out of `install` uncaught.
- The `/End` → `/Run` race under `MultipleInstances IgnoreNew` is now deterministic: `endTask()` polls `taskState()` until the instance actually stops, with a 10 s deadline checked every iteration, a 15 s timeout on the PowerShell calls so a wedged shell cannot hold it open, and an immediate exit when no PowerShell can answer at all.
- `stop` is idempotent like `restart` and `uninstall`, instead of throwing when nothing is installed.

## On testing the ordering off Windows

`schtasks.exe` and `powershell.exe` don't exist on macOS, so every scheduler call normally fails and the ordering between them is invisible — which is why this regression was invisible too. The new tests put executable stubs of those names first on `PATH`, which makes the call sequence observable and lets a chosen call fail on demand. That's the only way to reach the recovery path without a Windows box in a restricted shell. All five fail against the previous commit.

## What now runs

`.github/workflows/python-lock.yml`, a 4-leg matrix with `fail-fast: false`:

| os | tool | python | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| ubuntu-latest | uv | 3.12 | what `uv venv --python 3.12` pins |
| ubuntu-latest | pip | 3.10 | the documented floor, and the only way to hit the `python_full_version < '3.11'` marker arm |
| windows-latest | uv | 3.12 | |
| windows-latest | pip | 3.10 | |

**The pip command is not written into the workflow.** A new `install-plan.mjs python-install-command <uv|pip> [posix|windows]` extracts it verbatim from `bin/install` / `install.ps1` using the same matcher `installerRequirementDrift` already uses, so the job cannot pass while the real installer fails. A test fails if the workflow ever spells a pip line itself.

`scripts/verify-python-lock.py` is one file so both platforms assert identically: pinned versions match `PYTHON_REQUIREMENTS`, both packages import, every `litellm[proxy]` extra is installed and satisfies its specifier, and the proxy actually starts and answers `/health/liveliness`. On failure it dumps litellm's output — which is where a marker-excluded module surfaces as an ImportError.

## Two bugs the negative control had, both caught before pushing

These are worth recording because both produced a *passing* test that verified nothing.

**The control was testing the wrong failure.** It appended a nonexistent package to the lock, and locally that "passed" — but pip had died on *resolution*, never reaching hash checking. Now it derives a real marker-free entry from the lock, strips its hashes, and greps the output for `hash`, so a resolution error cannot pass for hash enforcement.

**Order matters, and the wrong order is silent.** Placed after the install, `uv pip install --require-hashes` on an already-satisfied requirement prints `Audited 1 package`, exits 0, and never looks at a hash. Reproduced exactly. The control now runs against the empty venv, before the install.

## Judgement calls

**paths filter, plus a weekly cron.** `paths:` is per-workflow, so gating inside `ci.yml` would gate `test` and `desktop` too. The filter's real risk is silently never running — and the case it structurally cannot see is PyPI changing under an unchanged lock — so `schedule: 17 6 * * 1` runs it weekly on main, plus `workflow_dispatch`.

**No macOS leg.** litellm 1.95.0 ships manylinux + win_amd64 wheels only, so macOS builds the sdist via maturin and Rust: minutes of compile, a toolchain to provision, and a failure mode belonging to the sdist rather than to the lock. It is also the one platform already verified by hand.

**No cache.** A lock-keyed cache can only hit when the lock is unchanged — the case needing no speed — and uv serves unpacked wheels from cache, so a hit could skip the very check the job performs. Same mechanism as the ordering bug above.

Thanks for the careful timeline and for separating this from #100 — the distinction you drew is exactly right, and the usage-log cross-check did most of the diagnostic work.

## What your evidence shows

One architectural point first, because it reframes the report: **native requests never touch the external-provider path.** A native turn goes from the router process straight to `chatgpt.com` — it does not pass through the gateway or anything `opencode-go`-related. The isolation you're asking for already exists per-request. What native and routed traffic *do* share is the router **process** itself, and that is where this incident lived:

- The 90 `opencode-go` 502s in your usage log are the gateway relaying a provider failure. Those were recorded normally and are a provider outage, not a router fault.
- The native 502s at 09:26:46, 10:07:27, 10:26:27 with **no matching usage event**, alongside `TypeError: fetch failed`, mean the router's own outbound connect to `chatgpt.com` failed at the socket level, before any response existed. On the commit you were running (`2941895`) a pre-header failure recorded no usage event — that gap was closed on main shortly after (the failure path now always meters, and a per-request timing line is logged even under quiet mode).
- `fetch failed` is the transport's generic wrapper; the code that says *why* (ECONNREFUSED, ENOTFOUND, connect timeout, …) lives on the error's `cause`, which the log line didn't print. That's why neither of us can say from the retained log whether this was DNS, ephemeral-port exhaustion, or something in between the machine and the edge.
- `Codex router exited (code=4294967295, signal=null)` is the router process dying with nothing logged about the cause — currently indistinguishable from an external kill (antivirus, OOM, job-object teardown).

## What's changing

Four fixes are landing on main:

1. **Cause-chain logging.** `request failed:` lines now walk the full `cause` chain, so the next occurrence logs e.g. `TypeError: fetch failed <- Error: connect ETIMEDOUT <addr> (ETIMEDOUT)` instead of stopping at the wrapper.
2. **More connect-level failures retried.** `ENOTFOUND`, `EADDRNOTAVAIL`, and `ENOBUFS` joined the bounded native retry set — all three fail before a connection exists (Windows produces them under connection churn), so a retry can never re-execute work.
3. **Every native failure meters.** The image/web-search path now records a usage event on failure too, so "failure with no usage event" stops being a possible state and stays meaningful as a diagnostic.
4. **Crash attribution.** The router now logs the full error chain and stack on an uncaught exception or unhandled rejection and exits with a distinct code (95/94). If the supervisor line ever shows one of those, it's an in-process router bug and the log above it names it; `4294967295` would then point to an external kill.

## If it happens again

Please update to latest main first, then capture:

1. The `[codex-router] request failed:` lines — they'll now name the socket-level code, which tells us DNS vs port exhaustion vs edge.
2. The `exited (code=…)` line — 94/95 means router bug (file it with the logged stack); anything else points outside the process.
3. `./model-router.ps1 codex support-bundle` output (path only, as before — it redacts the managed endpoint for you).

Pushed `635e1c9`. Two things resolved, one needs your call.

## Windows CI failure — fixed, and it was a real bug

The Windows leg rejected the command line outright:

```
cmd.exe /d /s /c "...\codex-doctor.cmd ^^^"debug^^^" ^^^"models^^^""
The syntax of the command is incorrect.
```

I was double-escaping `^` for every batch file. Only one shim shape needs that second layer — the cmd-shim npm generates under `node_modules/.bin`, which re-enters `cmd.exe` to reach the real program, so the first interpreter consumes a layer before the second sees it. The global npm shim this router actually meets (in `%APPDATA%\npm`) reaches its program without a nested interpreter and takes one layer.

**This is exactly the gap I flagged as unverified when I opened the PR, and the reason was structural:** every escaping test asserted the *shape of a command line nobody runs*, so a plausible-looking string sailed through. Two Windows-only tests now build a real shim — a plain batch file and npm's actual global template — push arguments containing spaces, quotes, `&`, `%` and `^` through it, and read back what the child received. Those would have failed on the first push.

## CodeQL — two of the three alerts are mine

`js/shell-command-injection-from-environment` at `codex-binary.mjs:76`, `doctor.mjs:103`, `agent-check.mjs:129`.

- **`codex-binary.mjs` predates this PR.** `main` already built a shell command from the same env-derived path — `codexSpawnTarget` returned `` command: `"${binary}"` `` with `shell: true`.
- **`doctor.mjs` and `agent-check.mjs` are new here.** Both previously spawned directly with no shell; routing them through `cmd.exe` is what introduced the flow.

CodeQL is factually right: a shell command line is built from a path sourced from `CODEX_BIN` / `LOCALAPPDATA` / `PATH`. My assessment is that it is low severity, because anyone who can set those already chooses which program runs — injection buys an attacker nothing they don't already have.

That said, escaping is the wrong last line of defence for a character that cannot occur in a real path, so `spawnableCommand` now **refuses** a command path containing `"`, `<`, `>`, `|`, `?`, `*`, or a control character — no Windows file name may hold any of them, and they are precisely the ones that could end the quoted span or start a second command. Legal-but-hostile characters (`C:\Program Files (x86)`, `Foo & Bar`) keep being escaped, since rejecting those would break ordinary installs.

**What I can't do:** that guard is unlikely to satisfy CodeQL, which won't recognise a custom validator as a sanitiser. Clearing the three alerts needs a dismissal in the Security tab, and whether that's the right call is yours — I'd rather leave them visible than paper over them. Say the word if you'd prefer a different approach.

Three separate problems in here. Two are fixed on main in #187, one was already fixed before you filed, and one of your suggested fixes would have made things worse — details below, because that last part matters if you were about to patch it locally.

**1. The enum type mismatch — fixed.**

This was the same root cause as #175. `namespace-relay.mjs` copied the client's tool schema to the provider verbatim, so nothing ever reconciled a literal with the type its own node declared. Note `appTaskLane` appears **nowhere in this repo** — it comes from your Codex build, and `mergeCodexAppTools` lets client-provided definitions win, so it could only ever be fixed at relay time, not in the bundled tool snapshot.

The fix drops literals that contradict their declared type rather than coercing them, which is where I ended up disagreeing with your experiment. You found that rewriting `enum: [true]` to `enum: ["true"]` under `type: "string"` produced 200s, and it does — but it tells the model to send the string `"true"` where the app expects a boolean. Since a literal that contradicts its own type could never validate anyway, dropping it can't change a well-formed schema. It is a widening (`"must be true"` becomes `"any string"`), which I'd rather have than a value the app never asked for.

**2. The 401/429 cooldowns — fixed, and the mechanism was not what it looked like.**

You were right that a 401 was surfacing as a rate limit, but the 401 wasn't being *mapped* to 429 anywhere. LiteLLM was taking the deployment out of rotation on the 401 and then answering later calls with its own synthetic 429 `No deployments available`. The router faithfully passed that along, and the correct 401 branch — which already existed and says "re-run setup" — was simply never reached.

Every model in the rendered gateway config has exactly one deployment (83 models, 83 unique upstream ids), so a cooldown could never route around a failure. It could only hide the cause. Fixed with `router_settings.disable_cooldowns`, so the real 401 reaches the translator.

Worth flagging: I first wrote a second layer that parsed the originating status out of LiteLLM's cooldown body. Review caught that it was dead code — `cooldown_handlers.py` reduces the cooldown list to bare deployment ids before it reaches the client, so that status is never on the wire. Removed. Mentioning it in case you were considering the same approach.

**3. The default baseUrl — already fixed before you filed.**

`config/kimi/kimi.json` moved to `https://api.moonshot.ai/v1` about 7.5 hours before this issue was opened. If you're on an older checkout, updating gets you that.

**4. Your suggested fix #2 — please don't apply it as written.**

Adding `api.kimi.com` to the allowed hosts in the balance probe would make it request `https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1/users/me/balance`, and that route doesn't exist on the coding endpoint. You'd turn a graceful "balance unavailable" into a thrown error.

The underlying issue is that an `sk-kimi-xk…` key is a **different product** from a Moonshot Open Platform key: it's the Kimi Platform coding subscription, which reports quota windows via `/usages` rather than a cash balance. Supporting it properly is a real change, not a host allowlist entry, and there's a second wrinkle — `config/kimi/api/kimi-k3.json` sends `upstreamModel: "kimi-k3"` while the coding endpoint expects `k3`. So setting only `KIMI_API_BASE_URL` leaves the wrong model id on the wire.

### CodeQL triage — the five `js/shell-command-injection-from-environment` alerts

Decision: **accept, not defects.** Evidence, since "the scanner is wrong" deserves more than an assertion:

1. **This PR removes shell usage; it adds none.** The diff deletes `return { command: `"${binary}"`, options: { shell: true } };` from the old resolution path. Grepping the branch for `shell: true` in the touched files returns exactly one hit — a *comment* at `src/agent-check.mjs:107` explaining why the code avoids it. Net change to shell surface is negative.
2. **Every flagged call site is a plain argv spawn.** `agent-check.mjs:123`, `doctor.mjs:98`, `grok-cli.mjs:100`, `codex-binary.mjs:72` all pass `(target.command, target.args, options)` with no `shell` key. On macOS and Linux `spawnableCommand` is an identity pass-through, so those three platforms have no shell in the path at all.
3. **The one genuine shell hop is deliberate and bounded.** A `.cmd`/`.bat` shim on win32 must go through `cmd.exe` — Node has refused to spawn one directly since CVE-2024-27980. That path uses an explicit `cmd.exe /d /s /c` with `windowsVerbatimArguments: true` and the repo's own escaping, not `shell: true`, precisely because Node's shell mode joins argv on spaces and would split a prompt sentence into eighteen arguments.
4. **The tainted source is guarded before it reaches escaping.** `assertSpawnablePath` throws on `/["<>|?*\^@-\^_]/` — the characters no Windows filename may contain and the ones that could close the quoted span. Rejecting rather than escaping is the right call for a path.
5. **Proven by execution, not string shape.** `test/spawnable-command.test.mjs` builds real `.cmd` shims (plain batch and npm's actual global-shim template) inside a directory named `shim dir (x86) & co`, spawns them with `C:\Program Files (x86)\thing`, `a&b`, `100%`, `caret^value`, and asserts on what the child received via its own `argv`. Confirmed in the `windows-latest` log that both ran for real and the suite reported 1031 pass / 0 fail.
6. The taint sources are `CODEX_BIN`, `GROK_CLI`, `LOCALAPPDATA` — set by the same principal who already controls what gets spawned. Someone who can set `CODEX_BIN` can simply point it at their own binary; there is no privilege boundary being crossed.

Alert #29 (`test/spawnable-command.test.mjs:172`) is a test-fixture false positive on `os.tmpdir()`.

**Both of your constraining findings are handled:**

1. *"Flattening the union is not enough — the root must literally be `type: "object"`."* `objectRootToolSchema` returns a merged plain object with no union keyword at all, not a flattened `oneOf`.

2. *"LiteLLM masks the union by stamping `type: "object"`."* That exact case is called out by name in `tool-schema-root.mjs:64`:

   > xAI's rule is about the root *keywords*, not the declared type: a schema may say `type: "object"` and still be rejected for carrying a `oneOf` beside it. Checking only `type`/`properties` here is what let the live client's `automation_update` — which sends both — through untouched.

**Your report did lead somewhere.** Probing that sanitizer with adversarial roots turned up a shape it *did* let through: `type: ["object", "null"]`. A nullable object root is legal JSON Schema, and `hasObjectRoot` accepted it because `properties` was present, so the declared type was never consulted.

Reviewed this from three angles (security of the retention store, correctness/regression against the aging work that landed in #239, and model-facing behavior). CI hadn't run — first-time-contributor approval was pending — so I also ran everything locally against a merge with current `main`.

## Fixed on this branch

**`npm test` was failing 9 tests on a stock macOS checkout**, which CI could not see. `ensureDirectoryPathWithoutLinks` validated the store by walking from the filesystem root and refusing any component that was a symlink. `/var` is a symlink to `/private/var` on every stock macOS install, so every path under `os.tmpdir()` traverses one — as do container bind mounts and symlinked home directories. GitHub's macOS runners hand out a temp path that happens not to cross a link, which is why CI stayed green while the same commit failed locally.

This mattered beyond the tests: in production the same check runs against the real `STATE_DIR`, so any install pointing state at `/tmp`, a bind mount, or a symlinked home would have had retention fail 100% of the time. Because retention correctly fails to the original result, it would have failed *quietly* — the feature simply never working, with no data loss to signal it.

Pushed `fix(retention)`: both that walk and the realpath-identity check in `assertPlainOwnedDirectory` now canonicalize first and compare against that. The guarantee that matters is unchanged — the directory written to is the one that was validated, and we own it — but a link the operator didn't plant is no longer treated as an attack. Your `retention rejects a symlinked state path before touching its target` test passes unchanged, and I added its counterpart covering the OS's own case. Suite is now **1319 passing, 0 failing, 13 skips** on the merged tree.

## Verified, no change needed

The `file-security.mjs` rework is a genuine fix, not just refactoring: the old `icacls /grant:r` only replaced the ACE for the named identity and left any pre-existing `Everyone`/`Users` grant in place, so this was a latent Windows over-permissioning bug affecting **every** private file the router writes — credentials and OAuth tokens included, not just retention. The replacement breaks inheritance, strips explicit ACEs, and `privateFileIsProtected` now fails closed unless exactly one owner rule matches.

Also confirmed by constructing the state files by hand rather than reading the code alone: an explicit **Off survives the upgrade** (only `defaultSettings()` changed), the env kill switch still wins, native aging stays default-off, #239's counters are intact and still written with `!== undefined` so a `0` survives, and a retention failure cannot propagate into the request path (guarded at both context creation and the `retain()` call).

## Two things worth your judgement before this ships

**1. The receipt no longer tells the model how to recover.** Today's receipt says *"Repeat the preceding <tool> call with the same arguments if exact or omitted content is needed."* That instruction is what commit `38b49fb` measured when it graduated aging out of experimental — the finding was specifically that models "re-run the tool instead of guessing when a compacted fact is requested." This PR removes that line and replaces it with four lines describing an owner-private retrieval the model explicitly cannot invoke ("No path, command, or retrieval capability is sent to the model"). So the validated recovery path is gone, and in its place is text inviting a model to believe exact bytes are obtainable when they aren't. The probe that measured the old behavior is rewritten in the same PR, and the description notes no provider calls were made, so the new design hasn't been re-validated the way the old one was.

The receipt header also roughly doubles, 331 → 653 bytes (~81 tokens per compacted result, ~4K tokens across 50 in a long session), on a feature whose purpose is saving context. About 110 of those bytes are a second copy of the same sha256 already printed on line one.

Suggestion: keep the re-run instruction and drop the three lines about the unreachable capability. That preserves the validated behavior and most of the token cost disappears.

**2. Retention is permanent by design.** There is no TTL, no purge command, and no `doctor`/uninstall integration — a silently growing (to 512 MiB) local archive of raw tool output, which in this product routinely includes file contents and command output. It is `0600`, owner-only, correctly excluded from support bundles, and the README is upfront about it. Still, this is the first time the router persists model-visible *content* to disk, where the established stance has been that telemetry records "counts and bytes... never the results." Turning that on by default is a product call I don't think a reviewer should make silently, so I'm flagging it rather than deciding it.

Everything technical is now green; these two are judgement, not defects.

## Windows is the only red job left

`test (windows-latest)` fails in `assertPlainOwnedDirectory`:

```
Error: Retained-result storage may not traverse a link.
    at assertPlainOwnedDirectory (src/tool-result-retention.mjs:175)
    at ensurePrivateDirectory (src/tool-result-retention.mjs:230)
```

macOS and Ubuntu are green, so this is Windows-specific to the identity comparison:

```js
normalizedRealPath(realpathSync.native(directory)) !==
normalizedRealPath(canonicalExistingPath(directory))
```

`realpathSync.native` normalizes 8.3 short names, and `canonicalExistingPath` walks components lexically, so it preserves whatever it was given. GitHub's Windows runners hand out a `TEMP` under `C:\Users\RUNNER~1\...`; realpath returns `C:\Users\runneradmin\...` and the lexical walk returns `RUNNER~1`, so the two sides differ and the guard fires even though nothing is wrong. I couldn't confirm the exact path from the log (it isn't printed), so treat that as the likely cause rather than a certainty — but the shape of the failure fits, and it's Windows-only.

If it is that, normalizing both sides fixes it without weakening anything, since `canonicalExistingPath` already rejects untrusted links before this point:

```js
normalizedRealPath(realpathSync.native(directory)) !==
normalizedRealPath(realpathSync.native(canonicalExistingPath(directory)))
```

## The receipt wording is worth a maintainer decision, not a tug-of-war

I see `Keep aged-result recovery non-executing` reverted my change and went further — the receipt now tells the model *"Do not repeat the tool call to recover omitted content. If exact content is needed, ask the owner."*

I understand the goal, and I'm not going to re-push against it. But it's worth flagging plainly: commit `38b49fb` graduated this feature out of experimental on the strength of an A/B whose finding was that models **re-run the tool** instead of guessing when a compacted fact is requested. That was the evidence that compaction was safe to enable. Instructing the model not to re-run removes that path, and "ask the owner" isn't available to an agent running unattended — which is the case aging matters most in. The likely outcome is the model guessing from head/tail, which is the failure the original wording existed to prevent.

There's a real tension here: you're protecting against a model treating a digest as a retrieval capability, which is a legitimate worry. But the two aren't in conflict — "repeat the call" and "the digest is not a retrieval handle" can both be true in the same receipt.

## What the test showed

With the branch installed and `microsoft_outlook_email` selected, the model does see the tools — asked to name them, Grok 4.6 listed `list_messages`, `draft_email`, and the rest. The relay also does its job: the call reaches Codex in the native shape.

Codex rejects it. Its tool router only dispatches tools it has actually loaded into the session, so a definition that arrives only in the outbound request is callable by the model and unknown to the client.

I checked this wasn't just a naming mistake on my side. A live capture of what the client sends showed connector namespaces are named for the connector alone, not `mcp__codex_apps__<connector>`:

```

```

The bug is real and this rules out the cheap fix. Of the three options I listed there, 1 and 2 are dead — no amount of definition merging makes these dispatchable. Only a router-side stand-in for `tool_search` can work, because the client has to be the one that loads the tool.

Codex executes `tool_search` itself, the same way it executes any other client-side tool. Relaying it to the provider as an ordinary function and mapping the model's call back to the native shape would let the model load a connector on demand and dispatch it on the next turn — which is exactly the native flow. Rejected inside a namespace the client already has, so this is not about a missing or misnamed namespace. Codex's tool router dispatches per *loaded tool*, and `tool_search` is what loads them. A definition that exists only in the outbound request is callable by the model and unknown to the client — which is a slightly worse failure than the status quo, because the model now confidently calls something that always errors.

This is the difference from `codex_app` that makes `mergeCodexAppTools` work there and not here: those tools are registered client-side with deferLoading and execute whether or not the definition was in the request. Connector tools are not.

## So the only lever is `tool_search`

Which reframes option 3. The router doesn't need to *answer* the search control, only to *translate* it — Codex executes `tool_search` itself, like any other client-side tool. Relayed to the provider as an ordinary function, with the model's call mapped back to the native shape on the way in, the model could load a connector on demand and dispatch it on the following turn. That is the native flow, and it needs no cache reading and no per-connector opt-in.

The open question is the native call shape `tool_search` expects, which I can't determine from outside the client.

The measurements in the original post still stand (171 tools, 649 KB, and the per-connector token costs), though they matter less now that wholesale merging is off the table.

Reviewed this against current `main` (it merges cleanly and `npm test` is 1339/0 failed with the merge in place). The design is right, and it is the same conclusion #253's author reached independently after disproving the definition-merging approach — the client has to be the one that loads the tool, so translating the control rather than answering it is the only door left. The fail-closed instincts throughout are good: `execution: "client"` gating so an unrelated function named `tool_search` never enables the relay, the deterministic alias on collision, live schemas winning a name collision, and `allowIncompleteToolSearch` scoped to `response.output_item.added`.

One defect, and I think it is load-bearing.

## Pairing is positional, so a batched search turn silently degrades

`flattenToolSearchHistory` matches a call to its output by **adjacency** (`input[index]` / `input[index + 1]`) and additionally requires `call_id` equality. When the model issues two `tool_search` calls in one turn, Codex emits them the way it emits any parallel tool calls — all calls, then all outputs — and adjacency never holds:

```js
const parallel = [
  { type:'tool_search_call',   execution:'client', call_id:'c1', arguments:{query:'mail'} },
  { type:'tool_search_call',   execution:'client', call_id:'c2', arguments:{query:'calendar'} },
  { type:'tool_search_output', execution:'client', call_id:'c1', tools:[{type:'function',name:'list_messages'}] },
  { type:'tool_search_output', execution:'client', call_id:'c2', tools:[{type:'function',name:'list_events'}] },
];
flattenToolSearchHistory(parallel, tools, namespaces);
// types after bridge: tool_search_call, tool_search_call, tool_search_output, tool_search_output
// tools added to request: 0
// flattened flag: false
```

Two consequences, and the second is the one that matters:

1. Four native Responses item types reach a chat-completions provider verbatim. Nothing downstream strips them — I grepped; `flattenToolSearchHistory` is the only code in `src/` that touches either type.
2. **Zero discovered tools are added to the request**, while the model has already been told in its own transcript that it discovered them. Its next call names a tool that is not in the tool list — which is the same "model can see it, client rejects it" failure this PR exists to fix, reintroduced through a different door.

The same thing happens to a pair split by remote compaction, in either direction:

```js
// output survived, its call did not  -> stays tool_search_output
// call survived, its output did not  -> stays tool_search_call
```

Both were returned unchanged in my run.

## Suggested fix

Pair by `call_id` rather than by position: walk the input once, record every well-formed `tool_search_call` id, and match each `tool_search_output` to a recorded id that appears **before** it. That keeps the property the adjacency tightening was reaching for — only matched, well-formed pairs replay, orphans never add tools — without making it positional. Orphans probably also want to be dropped rather than forwarded, since a native item type in a chat-completions body is not something the provider can do anything with.

Worth a test for the batched shape either way; the current suite only exercises the adjacent one, which is why this passes 35/35 today.

## Smaller notes

- `providerVisibleToolNames` is computed once before the `map`, then mutated as outputs are accepted. That is correct for "earlier discovery wins", but it does mean two outputs discovering the same tool report it in the first `function_call_output` and omit it from the second. Probably what you want; worth a comment saying so, because the omission reads as a bug from the model's side.
- The non-streaming path (`namespace-relay.mjs:594`) correctly omits `allowIncompleteToolSearch`, so a malformed-argument call stays an ordinary `function_call` there. That degrades to an "unsupported call" at the client rather than a malformed `tool_search_call`, which is the right trade — but it is silent. A log line would make it diagnosable.

## The parser fixes are right, and I would take them today

The old streaming path only handled `response.output_item.added` with `item.type === "function_call"`. It handled none of:

- a `function_call` that appears only in `output_item.done`
- `custom_tool_call` at all
- a final SSE block with no trailing blank line

Any one of those produces exactly the reported symptom — visible text, zero tool calls, `finish_reason: "stop"`, high output tokens. The rest of the repo already treats all three as normal upstream shapes (`empty-completion-guard.mjs:32,125,139`, `subagent-completion.mjs:138`, `gemini-shape.mjs:395`); the grok-oauth forwarder was the outlier. Your own new tests are the evidence for this.

**If you split the parser/mapping fixes into their own PR, I will merge it as-is.** That is roughly two thirds of the diff and it is low-risk.

## What blocks the retry heuristic

**1. It fires when the request offered no tools at all.** `isProgressOnlyStop` (`src/grok-oauth-turn.mjs:27`) never looks at `chat.tools`, and `handleChatCompletions` calls it unconditionally. Reproduced here: a request with no `tools` array, a 2-character answer, and `output_tokens: 1660` triggers a second full upstream call carrying "Continue the same task by calling tools now." The `completion_tokens >= 400` floor does not discriminate, because for Grok `output_tokens` *includes* reasoning tokens — so any reasoning-heavy short answer gets re-rolled. Please gate on the request actually offering tools.

**2. The first attempt's answer is discarded.** `turn = second` replaces attempt 1 whenever attempt 2 has any non-empty text. Please make the retry additive, or keep attempt 1 when attempt 2 also produces no tool calls.

**3. Streaming is replaced by an unbounded hold.** `collectUpstreamTurn` buffers the entire upstream turn before writing a byte, so grok-oauth streaming becomes cosmetic. `src/empty-completion-guard.mjs` caps exactly this at `MAX_PRECONTENT_BYTES = 1 MiB` / `MAX_PRECONTENT_MS = 30_000`, with a comment recording that an unbounded hold moved first-byte from 517 ms to 30,638 ms on a reasoning model. On your own repro (1660 hidden output tokens) this is tens of seconds of dead air per turn. Please apply the same caps and liveness release.

**4. The retry is silent and unmetered.** AGENTS.md's retry rule 6 says a silent retry is worse than no retry: the log line must not be gated on `CODEX_ROUTER_QUIET`, and the usage event must carry `retries`. Right now attempt 1's usage — ~106k input + 1660 output in your repro — is dropped, so `usage-events.jsonl` under-reports a turn the account was billed for twice. Compare `emptyCompletionRetried`, which exists so `context-window-drift.mjs:42` can ignore the doubled prompt.

**5. No kill switch.** Please add one matching `CODEX_ROUTER_EMPTY_COMPLETION_RETRY` (`src/router.mjs:157`). The 120/400 thresholds are currently hardcoded with no override.

**6. The retry body is not drained on failure.** `if (retried.ok && retried.body)` leaves a non-ok response unread and uncancelled.

- `ToolSpec::ToolSearch { execution, description, parameters }` — all three non-`Option`, always serialized
- `execution: "client"` is a literal in `tool_search_spec.rs`
- `ToolSearchCall.arguments` is a `serde_json::Value`, i.e. an object and not a JSON string; `status` is optional, so stripping it is safe
- `ToolSearchOutput { call_id, status, execution, tools }`
- output entries are `LoadableToolSpec::{Namespace, Function}`, and namespace children are tagged `type: "function"`

Confirmed, and the cause of the loop is fixed on main in #274. Leaving this open for points 1 and 2 — see below.

**What was actually wrong.** `curate-models` stored `contextWindow: 131072` for every model it added, even though `discover-models` had already fetched the catalog record saying `context_length: 1050000` — discovery was parsing out the ids and throwing the rest away. Codex derives its compaction threshold from that stored number, so your 1.05M model was told to summarize at 110,000, and the high-erring estimate cleared that on every turn. Discovery now reads the advertised size (`context_length`, the served figure under `top_provider`, `context_window`, or Copilot's `capabilities.limits.max_context_window_tokens`, taking the smallest present since those are limits at different scopes), and both curation forms store it with `autoCompact` derived at 85%. Only a model the catalog sizes in silence still falls back to 131072.

**Your existing entry will not be rewritten.** An additive `--models` run deliberately never clobbers metadata a user may have hand-tuned, so your workaround remains the right repair. It is now documented in TROUBLESHOOTING under "A session compacts on every turn instead of getting work done"; `--remove` followed by re-curating also works.

**Points 1 and 2 are deliberately still open.** Your ~3.9x measurement holds up against the numbers in your own log — roughly 382 KB of serialized body over ~29.5K real prompt tokens, so about 13 real bytes per token rather than the `ESTIMATE_BYTES_PER_TOKEN = 3.3` in `src/response-usage.mjs:26`. That constant is calibrated against model-visible text, while `estimateInputTokens` measures the entire routed body including re-sent tool schemas, JSON escaping and `encrypted_content` reasoning blobs. Recalibrating it without a captured Responses payload to measure against would just be a different guess, and the two error directions are not symmetric: an estimate that lands low lets the provider reject the turn outright.

Worth correcting one thing in the original report, though: the `Math.min(estimate, contextWindow)` clamp never fired in your session. 115,762 was already under the declared 131,072, so the compaction came from the threshold being too low, not from the clamp. The clamp is still worth revisiting — since `autoCompact` is 85% of the window, any clamped estimate sits above the compaction threshold by construction — but it is a separate latent problem, not what you hit.

If you have a captured payload from one of these turns, that would let us fix point 2 properly instead of swapping one guess for another.
