The gateway crash itself is LiteLLM's, but what turned it into a dead session was ours. `src/start.mjs` raced every child's exit as service death, so when the proxy exited 1 the router **and all three forwarders** were SIGTERM'd with it — which is exactly why clients saw a bare `Connection error` with nothing in it naming the gateway.

The gateway is now supervised in place: doubling backoff (1/2/4/8/16 s, capped at 30 s), at most 5 restarts in a 10-minute sliding window, with the router still listening throughout. A crash now costs one stalled request instead of the session. Past that bound the service still exits, so launchd / systemd / Task Scheduler get their clean restart as before. `/health` carries `degraded: ["gateway"]`, so `doctor` says "serving but reports gateway unreachable" rather than a flat "not ready". `CODEX_ROUTER_GATEWAY_RESTARTS=0` restores the old behaviour if you want it.

**A bonus bug, found by CI on the regression test.** The Windows job failed, and the cause was a real production defect rather than test scaffolding: `run()` in `src/start.mjs` used a bare `spawn(command, args)`, and Node has refused to spawn a `.cmd`/`.bat` without a shell since the CVE-2024-27980 fix (18.20.2 / 20.12.2 / 21.7.3), throwing EINVAL synchronously. This repo already documents that trap in `src/spawnable-command.mjs`; `start.mjs` was simply a call site that had missed it. So a Windows operator pointing `MODEL_ROUTER_LITELLM_BIN` at a batch wrapper would have killed the whole service before it spawned anything. It is inert for normal installs — the installer produces `litellm.exe` and our Node children resolve to `process.execPath`, both non-batch — but it is fixed now, with a source guard so a future refactor cannot quietly reintroduce it on a platform CI would only catch late.

CI is red on `test` for **all three platforms** on `ce9b742` — five tests in `test/gemini-surface.test.mjs`, every one that relays a turn. Root cause found, and it is not a rebase artifact:

**`src/gemini-surface.mjs:183` — `signal: request.signal`**

This is the only `request.signal` in the repository. CI runs **Node v24.19.0**, where `http.IncomingMessage` exposes a `signal` that has **already aborted** by the time the handler finishes `readRequestBody` and issues the loopback fetch. `fetch` throws `AbortError` immediately, the bare `catch {}` two lines down swallows it, and every turn becomes `502 "The local model router could not be reached."` The upstream never receives a request at all.

Reproduced by exact signature: shimming an aborted `IncomingMessage.prototype.signal` on Node 22 produces all five failures in the same order with the same messages — `502 !== 200`, `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'headers')`, `502 !== 200`, `…(reading 'candidates')`, `502 !== 429`.

**Why local runs look fine.** Node 22.23.1 and 25.6.0 lack the property entirely, and 26.7.0 has it non-aborted at that point. Only the Node 24 LTS line is affected. A green local suite is not evidence against this.

**Why it matters beyond CI.** `package.json` declares `"node": ">=22.19.0"`, so Node 24 is a supported runtime. On Node 24 the Gemini integration 502s on every single turn — the feature is non-functional there, not merely untested.

**Fix options**, in increasing order of correctness:

1. Guard it — `signal: request.signal?.aborted ? undefined : request.signal`. Verified: restores 13/13 under the Node-24 shim.
2. Drop `request.signal` entirely.
3. Wire an explicit `AbortController` off the response's `close` event.

Option 1 is the minimal unblock, but 2 or 3 is probably the right end state, since the current line cannot do what it intends on Node 24 anyway — it aborts the loopback fetch before it is ever issued rather than cancelling a genuinely abandoned turn.

## Why

`cursor-agent` is an agent, not a model endpoint. It prepends its own harness to every request, and that cannot be turned off on a standard plan.

Measured on live turns:

| Prompt sent | `prompt_tokens` billed |
|---|---|
| ~20 tokens ("What is 17 times 23?") | **22,166** |
| ~12 tokens ("Reply with exactly: …") | **22,162** |

A fixed floor of roughly **22,150 input tokens per turn**, whatever you ask. The same question to a normal provider bills ~20. On a plan denominated in credits tied to API cost, that is about a thousandfold markup on short prompts.

Two hidden flags looked like they would fix it. Both are refused by Cursor's backend, not the CLI:

- `--exclude-workspace-context` → `[invalid_argument] Workspace context exclusion is not allowed for this user, team, or selected model`
- `--system-prompt <file>` → `[invalid_argument] unknown option '--system-prompt'`

They are internal or enterprise-gated. There is no other route: Cursor publishes no inference API, and `--endpoint` speaks their own protocol.

Combined with the limitation already documented here — cursor-agent never emits OpenAI `tool_calls`, so these models cannot drive an agentic Codex turn — what remains is a provider that costs ~22K tokens a turn to answer questions and cannot do the main job. Not worth shipping.

## Worth keeping from this

Verified facts, so nobody re-derives them:

1. **Cursor CLI cannot be a router target.** No BYOK, no custom base URL. `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` has no endpoint keys, `--endpoint` speaks Cursor's own protocol, Bedrock mode validates against Cursor's backend, and the IDE's "Override OpenAI Base URL" is IDE-only and refuses private addresses.
2. **Cursor CLI as a provider costs ~22,150 prompt tokens per turn**, unavoidably, and the flags that would reduce it are server-gated.
3. **`cursor-agent` never emits OpenAI tool calls**, so it cannot drive Codex turns regardless of cost.

Also learned, and applicable beyond Cursor: `--stream-partial-output` does not replace cursor-agent's message-level emitter, it runs beside it, so naive concatenation doubles the output; usage is reported as camelCase in live results but snake_case in the bundle; and `--trust` is mandatory for any directory the CLI has not seen.

The branch is kept locally. Reopen from `feat/cursor-cli-provider-main` if Cursor ever exposes a raw endpoint or ungates the harness flags.

Points 1 and 2 are now fixed in #281, so this issue is fully closed out.

**Point 2 turned out not to need a new divisor — the constant was right, its input was not.**

`estimateInputTokens` measured the whole serialized body, and most of a body that reaches us is `encrypted_content`: the sealed chain of thought on each reasoning item. Those bytes buy zero prompt tokens on the routed path — the gateway's Responses→Chat bridge drops reasoning items outright, and a Responses-native routed provider cannot decrypt another vendor's token — but they were charged at 3.3 bytes each along with everything else.

Measured through the router itself on a twelve-turn tool loop, there is a sharp condition on it. `carryReasoningThroughInput` already rewrites a reasoning item into assistant text when it carries summary text, and the ciphertext leaves with it: **0 of 12 blobs reach the gateway.** An item with an empty summary — what a provider returns when it has none to give — is forwarded whole: **12 of 12 blobs reach the gateway, and they are 64% of the body we send.** Charging that 64% at 3.3 is where your 3.9x comes from, and it explains why this bites some sessions and not others.

Your own figures pin it independently: 382 KB over 29,551 tokens is 12.9 real bytes per token, and since visible text cannot exceed about 4 bytes per token, at least 69% of that body was not something the model read. No captured payload needed after all.

The other two candidates were measured and ruled out. JSON escaping is 0.2–3% of the body and structural scaffolding 1–5% — too small to matter. Tool schemas are 4–13%, appear once rather than being multiplied, and are genuinely prompt tokens, so they stay counted.

The estimate now subtracts `encrypted_content` and counts everything else. The subtraction is deliberately one-sided — subtract what is provably invisible rather than sum what is visible — so an unrecognized field, a compressed frame or a malformed body is counted whole and errs high, which is the direction that keeps a provider from rejecting the turn.

**On point 1, the clamp stays, but you were right that it was a latent guarantee.** It used to fire on conversations nowhere near the limit: a body three quarters ciphertext crossed the window at a quarter of its real size, and because `autoCompact` is 85% of the window, a clamped estimate compacted by construction. Counting only model-visible bytes puts a floor under it — the estimate can only reach the window if the visible text does, so a clamped estimate now means the conversation really is between 82.5% and 100% of the window, where compacting is the right answer. Clamping lower would skip a compaction that is genuinely due and hand the next turn to the provider to reject.

One thing left deliberately wrong, and wrong upward: base64 image data is still counted at the byte rate, which is far above what an image really costs. That cost is a per-provider tiling formula, and inventing one would be exactly the guess we declined to make about the divisor. It is the remaining source of spurious clamping — worth its own issue if you hit it.

Regression coverage runs end to end through a real router process against the body it actually forwards, with a premise assertion that the body really carried the blobs, so it cannot pass vacuously.

Half (b) is implemented in #284, so both halves are now done and this can close.

**1. A 400/422 now demotes a `proven` slug, on one occurrence.** The gate was the defect, not the thresholds. `observeSubagentOutcome` gated on `awaitingSpawnProof` — true only for `experimental` — so promotion on turn one closed the demotion path with it, and the oldest observation on the wire beat every later one. The gate is now revocability (`spawnProofRevocable`: experimental **or** proven); promotion stays scoped to the experimental window, because a first clean turn is only news once.

One occurrence rather than a repeat, because promotion is one occurrence and the experimental demotion already required only one — a slug that just passed the two-request live probe is demoted by a single 400 today, and nothing makes that 400 weaker after a 200. Transients (401/402/403/408/429/5xx) were already excluded and stay excluded. Registry-`v2` models are untouched: their claim is the shipped native collaboration proof, not this machine's traffic. Re-promotion needed no change and stays manual — `subagentVerificationCandidates` does not skip `failed`, so `control subagents verify` or a switch off-and-on re-researches with live requests. Demotion is automatic; the direction that spends quota stays under your hand.

**2. The ceiling is in tokens, not turns, and it is derived rather than invented.** There is no turn-shaped number anywhere in the repo — `max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 6` is width not depth, `turnLimit` in `codex-app-tools.mjs` is pagination, `MAX_DEPTH = 8` is schema recursion — and no test or fixture has ever run a child for more than one turn. Any N would have been made up.

But `context-window-drift.mjs` already names this exact pathology: a task that opens above its compaction threshold, summarizes, redoes the same opening work "and compact[s] again without ever finishing… The session simply never ends." That sentence supplies both the unit and the multiple. The unit is the model's own `autoCompact` budget, already in the catalog and published by the provider; one budget is a large but legitimate task, and it is compacting *again* that is the runaway.

So `src/subagent-turns.mjs` accounts each spawn by `thread-id` and sums the **new** input tokens it produces — every child turn resends the whole conversation, so growth in the prompt count is what the child newly made, and a compaction makes the count fall, so everything after it is work being done twice. The ceiling is twice the larger of the declared `autoCompact` and the largest prompt that spawn has actually had accepted.

That second term is what makes a false demotion impossible rather than merely unlikely: an uncompacted spawn's total is exactly half its own ceiling however long its task runs, so neither a model whose declared budget sits far below its window (the validator only requires `1 ≤ autoCompact ≤ contextWindow`) nor a single oversized tool result can condemn anything. Only counts the provider actually reported move the total; substituted estimates and retry-doubled counts are refused via the same `acceptedInputTokens` predicate `context-window-drift.mjs` uses. A model declaring no `autoCompact` is counted and never condemned.

**On "terminal turn": there is no positive detector and none is needed.** The turn that ended a spawn is only knowable by no further turn arriving — but a ceiling can only ever be crossed by a spawn that is *still producing turns*, which is the same statement as "this has not converged". A converged child stops, and a spawn that stopped never reaches the ceiling. The worry about telling an intermediate no-tool-call turn from a final one therefore never has to be resolved.

A child thread reused for a `FOLLOWUP_TASK` is deliberately one spawn — its context genuinely carries across — and an idle one expires at 15 minutes.

Both demotions log unconditionally and record the turn and token counts in the proofs file, so `control subagents status` and the tray say what happened instead of a picker entry quietly disappearing. The intentional promote-on-first-turn e2e is untouched.

The TTL is merged in #283, so all three asks from this issue are now done and it can close.

**Retained results expire after 7 days.** The number is derived rather than round. Nothing ever reads those bytes back into a turn — the receipt tells the model to repeat the tool call — so a retained original's only reader is you, forensically, and only while the session that produced it still matters. The caps say the same about intent: 512 files and 512 MiB against a 32 KiB compaction floor is a working set of a few long sessions, not a history. And a week is already this repo's "recent enough to still act on" horizon, in `AUTO_ANNOUNCE_WINDOW_MS` and `SIZE_CACHE_TTL_MS` alike.

**Nothing sweeps on a timer, and nothing is added to startup.** Entries expire when the store is next written to — the way `writeCooldownDocument` trims the cooldown store on its next write, and the way a provider cooldown reads as gone long before anything deletes it. `doctor` therefore reports what has *already* aged out rather than what was removed, and never deletes. `./bin/control tool-result-aging purge --expired` runs that same sweep by hand, which is what an install needs when compaction is off and nothing is going to write again. Same `--yes` consent, same `--dry-run`, same containment as a full purge, and it never removes `.retention-key`, since expiring that would orphan the entries the TTL just decided to keep. On a TTL of off it refuses rather than quietly emptying the store.

`./bin/control tool-result-aging ttl <days|off|default>` sets the lifetime, in the same versioned state file the aging toggles use. `off` is a real answer and is kept verbatim; a state file written before the TTL existed never answered the question, so it reads as the default. `CODEX_ROUTER_TOOL_RESULT_AGING=0` still does not disable expiry — it stops the router rewriting request context, while expiry is hygiene for bytes already on disk.

This also closes the cap complaint directly: a store parked at 512 files now drains itself a week later instead of staying permanently full.

**On the standing caveat — I looked into why #245 is closed.** It was closed by its author, both the upstream PR and their fork mirror, nine seconds apart, with no closing comment, six minutes after they posted the Windows 8.3 fix and said they were waiting on a CI run that was still blocked on maintainer approval for an external branch. Not a wrong-approach rejection and not superseded: there is no successor PR or issue, and nothing else references it. So nothing on main writes to `retained-tool-results` yet, and this TTL manages the same store the purge and the doctor row already do. If you want that work back, the blocker looks like process rather than code.

It is built to fit a reland rather than to preempt it: `expireRetainedToolResults` is the call the writer's pre-write cap scan already has the directory listing for, path resolution and name shapes are unchanged, and the key is left alone. Two things a reland should know — the aging state file gained a `retentionTtlDays` field that both existing setters now preserve, so a rewrite of that module must keep threading it; and expiry ages by mtime, so if an owner-retrieval feature ever touches mtime on read, the TTL becomes "since last access", which should be a deliberate call rather than an inherited one.

**The probe is much better now — a single run gives a verdict, not a vibe.** #285 is merged, so everything below is on `main`.

Nobody here has a Devin account, so the whole Cascade transport is still inference from a shipped binary. What changed is that the probe no longer hides that. The old one printed a line per stage, and each line could pass while the thing it was meant to prove had failed — an account that decoded to zero models printed `OK: account advertises 0 model(s)`, which is the exact symptom of a renumbered field. Worse, a tool call arriving under a field number this build doesn't know was skipped in silence and reported as *"this model cannot drive a Codex turn"* — blaming your model for our bug.

Now every assumption gets its own PASS/FAIL line with the value that actually came back, and a `VERDICT` at the end that can be INCONCLUSIVE — a run that reached nothing is no longer a pass. If a tool call goes missing, three separate lines distinguish "the field moved" from "the model declined", including the decisive one:

```
FAIL  tool calls decoded: the upstream reported a function-call stop reason and this build
      decoded no tool call — calls are being dropped on the wire, not declined by the model
      observed: stopReason=10; undecoded fields: field 19 (length-delimited, 27B over 1) -> UNKNOWN
```

## To run it

```sh
git clone https://github.com/duolahypercho/codex-router && cd codex-router
npm install

./bin/devin-probe                  # free — reads your session, lists your models
./bin/devin-probe --live --tools   # one short turn, capped at 64 output tokens
```

You need `devin auth login` done first, and Node 22.19+. The probe never installs the router, starts a service, or changes any config — it reads the session file the Devin CLI already wrote and talks to Cognition directly. It caps itself at 64 output tokens and 90 seconds, so the live run costs essentially nothing. A mistyped flag now fails the run instead of quietly skipping the test it names.

**At the end it prints a fenced block. Copy that whole block here.** It carries the checklist plus your Node/OS/`devin` CLI version — the version matters, since the field numbers were derived from build `3000.4.25`. It deliberately carries no token, no full path (`$HOME` is folded to `~`), and no response content beyond the fixed test prompt's answer.

Please also say which plan you're on (Core / Team / Enterprise). `disable_cascade` and `allowed_model_uids` are team settings that can refuse the whole thing, and that would look like a transport bug if we didn't know.

**A failure is just as useful as a success** — arguably more. The `observed:` lines are the point: `connect-code=invalid_argument` with the upstream's message names the field we got wrong, and `-> UNKNOWN` in a census line names a field number that moved. Either one is worth more to us than a green run.

Full walkthrough, including what every failure line means, is in [`docs/DEVIN-CLI-PROBE.md`](docs/DEVIN-CLI-PROBE.md).

Not user error — this is a router bug, and it is fixed on main in #288. Thanks for the exact error text; it named the field, which made this a short hunt.

**What was happening.** When web search is on, Codex declares a hosted search tool on *every* request, whether or not the model ends up searching — which is why "running anything" was literal. Codex sends the current OpenAI spelling of that tool, `{"type": "web_search", …, "search_content_types": [...]}`. I confirmed that against the shipped 0.147 binary: its field table reads `web_search | external_web_access | indexed_web_access | filters | user_location | search_context_size | search_content_types`, and the string `web_search_preview` does not appear in the binary at all. Meta's Responses endpoint validates against the older schema, where `search_content_types` belongs only on `web_search_preview`, so it rejected the request outright. The router was forwarding the tool list verbatim.

Nothing to do with your config. Turning web search off in Codex would have been a workaround, not a fix.

**Worth knowing which side is behind.** The field is spec-valid where Codex puts it — OpenAI documents `search_content_types` on `web_search`, while `web_search_preview` is the legacy tool documented with only `type` and `sources`. So this is Meta running an older copy of the schema rather than being strict about it. That is why the fix is scoped to Meta only: the router now drops just `search_content_types` from Meta-bound requests, keeps the search tool and every other setting on it, and leaves the field alone for all other providers. If you ever send Meta a genuine `web_search_preview` tool, the field stays on it.

All three Meta models share the one endpoint, so Muse Spark 1.1, 1.2 and 1.2 Contributor are all covered.

**One thing I cannot rule out from here.** I only have evidence for this single field. If Meta's schema copy is older in other ways too, you may hit a second 400 naming a different `tools[]` field — `filters` and `external_web_access` are the likely candidates. If that happens, please paste the new error and I will extend the same correction. I deliberately did not pre-emptively strip those, since that would be guessing at a shape rather than correcting an observed rejection.

Point 3 is not met, though, and it is a **data-loss regression** rather than a gap. Three blockers below, then two smaller items.

## Blocker 1 — held streaming deltas are dropped

The final `emitPendingDeltas()` at `src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs:545` returns immediately because `holding` is still `true` — nothing clears it after `consumeResponsesStream` returns. `beginStream()` on the next line then sets `holding = false`, writes the head and role chunk, and the code proceeds straight to the finish chunk. **Every buffered delta is discarded.**

Reproduced with three probes against your head:

- **Streaming, tools offered, short answer** (`"Done."`, 5 output tokens, no retry): client receives role chunk → `finish_reason: "stop"` → usage → `[DONE]`. The answer text never arrives. The same request on the merge base `16b68f7` streams `{"content":"Done."}` correctly — so this is introduced here, on the most common shape there is, since Codex always offers tools.
- **Streaming + retry preferred**: `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` with **zero tool_call deltas** — a protocol-invalid response.
- **Streaming + keep-first**: the first answer's text is dropped.

One-line fix, verified: insert `releaseHold();` before the `emitPendingDeltas()` at line 545. All three probes then pass.

The suite stays green because **every retry test in this PR uses `stream: false`** (the non-stream path reads `turn.contentText`, not `turn.deltas`), and the two pre-existing streaming tests either offer no tools (`:451`, so the hold never arms) or emit a tool call that releases it (`:515`). Please add streaming coverage for all three shapes above.

## Blocker 2 — the liveness design, which I have to push back on harder than "stated plainly"

It is worse than the PR describes, because `beginStream()` is what calls `response.writeHead(200)`. Holding means the client gets **no HTTP response head at all** — not a silent stream, a silent socket.

And the forwarder handles no reasoning events whatsoever (`applyResponsesEvent`, `grok-oauth-turn.mjs:208-255`, has no reasoning case), so during Grok's thinking phase there are no deltas at all, `shouldReleaseProgressOnlyHold` cannot fire, and 1 MiB of raw SSE is far more than a reasoning summary produces. The only releases that matter are the first visible token / tool call, or the 30 s cap.

Measured against a backend that reasons for 3 s then answers:

```
no tools  : first byte 25 ms
with tools: first byte 3,070 ms
```

Time-to-first-byte becomes the model's full thinking latency. grok-4.6 ships `defaultEffort: "high"` with `xhigh` available, and your own fixture is 1,620 reasoning tokens against 40 visible ones — so the cap is reached routinely, not in the tail. This is the same regression `empty-completion-guard.mjs:64-73` already measured and rejected (517 ms → 30,638 ms), reintroduced on a model chosen for reasoning depth. It also inflates `firstTokenMs` on every held turn, and non-retried held turns are not excluded by `provider-usage.mjs`'s `measurable` gate, so grok-4.6 would start reporting a fabricated multi-second TTFT in the meter.

Traded against the bug being fixed — one wasted round trip when Grok says "Next I will update the deck." and stops — 30 s of dead air on the common path is the worse deal. Codex will not hard-fail (undici defaults to 300 s, `router.mjs:3253` sets `requestTimeout = 0`, and `upstream-retry.mjs` only retries pre-header transport failures), so this is a UX cost rather than a correctness one — but it is paid by every turn to buy a fix for a rare one.

**There is a hold-free design available, and I would rather have it.** Chat Completions permits `tool_calls` deltas after `content` deltas within one choice. Stream attempt 1 live; if it stops progress-only, run the retry and *append* its tool-call deltas plus `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` to the same open stream, discarding the retry's text. The client sees the status sentence followed by the tool call — the outcome you want — at zero added latency, and `finish_reason` is only written at the end so nothing is finalized prematurely.

Failing that, gate the hold on evidence: only hold a conversation that has already shown a progress-only stop on this `x-grok-conv-id`, so the dead air is paid only by sessions actually exhibiting the bug.

## What I found and fixed

`isProgressOnlyStop` matches a *shape*, and no better signal exists in the turn — so a **finished** task also matches it. "Yes, that is correct." after 1,500 reasoning tokens is byte-for-byte a turn that stopped after "Next I will update the deck.". Since grok-4.6 reasons by default, the `output_tokens` floor is met on essentially every turn and the 120-character limit is what actually decides. Short final answers are common, so this fires on the common path, not in the tail.

A wasted round trip would be fine. The nudge made it worse than that:

```
"Continue the same task by calling tools now."
```

That gives the model no way to say the task is done. Probed against a mock backend — turn 1 answers `"Yes, that is correct."` (1,500 output / 1,490 reasoning), retry gets the nudge:

```
finish_reason = tool_calls
content       = "Yes, that is correct."
tool_calls    = [{"function":{"name":"exec_command","arguments":"{\"cmd\":\"ls\"}"}}]
```

`shouldPreferRetryTurn` grafts a call the model never proposed onto a finished answer, and Codex runs it. The same happens to a hosted-search-only turn — `web_search_call` is not in `TOOL_ITEM_TYPES`, so a searched-and-answered turn is retried too (probe: `attempts=2`).

**The fix is the nudge wording, not new control flow** — offering the no-tool branch first routes the finished case into the keep-first path you already built and tested:

```js
const PROGRESS_ONLY_NUDGE =
  "If your previous message already completed the task, restate the final answer " +
  "and call no tool. Otherwise continue the same task now by calling the tools you need.";
```

A false positive now costs one round trip instead of a wrong action. Added `a finished task answered in one line declines the retry instead of calling a tool`, which asserts `finish_reason: "stop"`, the first answer intact, no `tool_calls`, and both attempts still billed with the marker set.

Also corrected the CHANGELOG and TROUBLESHOOTING wording: both said "a genuine progress-only stop", which claims a diagnosis the code cannot make. They now state plainly which turns pay for the retry and which knobs narrow it.

The review found several correctness and security blockers:

- The CLI and documentation support `--api-key KEY`, which places provider secrets in process arguments. Router policy requires hidden interactive input so keys do not enter argv, logs, shell history, or tracked snippets.
- Rotation is only applied to the next request. The forwarder relays the failing 401/402/403/429 response after marking cooldown, so the PR does not provide the same-turn recovery described in its automatic-rotation behavior.
- Pool metadata can name an arbitrary credential `file`; reads are not constrained back beneath the router state directory. A damaged or tampered metadata file could therefore cause an unrelated local file to be used as an outbound credential.
- Pool state, counters, cooldowns, and member secrets are mutated without the repository's cross-process transaction/lock discipline, so concurrent CLI and forwarder writers can lose state.
- Error classification uses an unbounded `upstream.clone().text()`, allowing an upstream to force the forwarder to buffer an arbitrarily large error body.
- The two broad tests do not exercise the real forwarder boundary, concurrent mutations, path confinement, or same-request behavior.

A credential pool needs a bounded in-request retry design, hidden-only secret entry, state-directory confinement, atomic cross-process mutation, bounded body inspection, and end-to-end forwarder tests before it can protect core routing behavior. Closing this version rather than merging a partial credential-management path.

## Root cause

`providerToolSchema` (`src/tool-schema-root.mjs:259`) does exactly two things: align literals with their declared type, and collapse a union/nullable **root**. A schema whose root is a plain object is returned by identity, with every `$ref` intact:

```js
if (!hasRootUnion(normalized) && !hasNullableObjectRoot(normalized)) return normalized;
```

`resolveRef` exists (`:27`) but is reachable only from `objectBranches`, which feeds the root collapse — it is never used to inline refs into the relayed copy.

The relay path confirms it: `src/namespace-relay.mjs` calls `providerToolSchema` at `:147`, `:172` and `:257` and nothing else. `src/oauth-forwarder.mjs` never touches `tools` — `normalizeKimiBody` only strips `client_metadata`, folds assistant messages, and remaps `reasoning_effort`. So `"$ref": "#/properties/filters/properties/priceRange"` reaches Moonshot verbatim and it 400s the whole request.

**One correction to your report:** Grok is not protected by a stronger `$ref` collapse. `src/grok-oauth-forwarder.mjs:359` uses `objectRootToolSchema(normalizeSchemaLiterals(...))`, which is a stronger *root* collapse but still preserves `$defs` and every `$ref`. Grok simply does not enforce Moonshot's `#/$defs/`-only rule. The rest of your chain is accurate.

## Not fixed by #363, despite appearances

#363 added `nonRecursiveToolSchema` (+178 lines in the same file), but it solves a different problem and is scoped away from kimi:

- It removes only **cycle-closing** back edges and deliberately preserves acyclic refs, with the comment *"expanding a shared ref DAG can grow exponentially."* A sibling-property `$ref` is acyclic, so it survives untouched.
- It is gated behind `repairToolSchemaRoots(tools, { nonRecursive: true })`, called only under `if (needsZenFreeToolCompatibility(route))`. kimi never reaches it.

Its rewritten `resolveRef` is a useful building block for the real fix though — it gained RFC 6901 fragment decoding, array-index traversal, and `Object.hasOwn` guards.

## Suggested fix

Add an exported `inlineForeignRefs(schema)` to `src/tool-schema-root.mjs` that walks the schema and, for any `$ref` not starting with `#/$defs/`, replaces the node with the resolved contents merged with the node's sibling constraints — bounded by `MAX_DEPTH` and a `seen` set, leaving unresolvable refs alone rather than guessing.

Then gate it per-provider rather than applying it everywhere: add a `{ inlineForeignRefs }` option mirroring the `{ nonRecursive }` flag #363 introduced, and switch it on for the kimi route. Applying it to all providers risks the combinatorial blowup that comment warns about and changes the wire payload for providers that work today. Cap the expansion size and fall back to the unmodified schema if the inlined result exceeds a byte budget.

**Tests it needs:** `test/tool-schema-root.test.mjs` for the transform — build a schema with `properties.filters.properties.inboundTotalDurationRange = { $ref: "#/properties/filters/properties/priceRange" }` and assert no `$ref` survives outside `#/$defs/` and that the inlined node carries `priceRange`'s constraints. Then `test/namespace-relay.test.mjs` for the wiring: relay that tool on the kimi route and assert the emitted `parameters` has no sibling `$ref`, while an unaffected provider's copy is returned by identity.

Reviewed this while clearing the PR queue. It's still a draft so no action is expected — but the findings are concrete enough to be worth passing on now rather than after you've built more on top.

The problem is real and worth fixing. The implementation has four independent ways to silently delete legitimate output, and silent deletion is the hardest failure to attribute back to its cause.

**1. The filter runs on every field of every event, including tool-call arguments.** `rewriteTextFields` (line 34) walks blindly into `item`, `part`, `output`, `content` with no `event.type` dispatch. That includes `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, which streams tool-call arguments as incremental JSON. Concrete break: MiniMax calls `apply_patch` on a file whose content mentions `<think>` — a prompt template, an SSE parser, documentation about this very feature. The filter eats from `<think` onward, the reassembled arguments are invalid JSON, and the tool call fails.

`src/zai-responses-compat.mjs:230` is the established pattern here: it dispatches on `event.type` explicitly. This should do the same, restricted to `response.output_text.delta` / `.done`.

**2. `this.#buffer.indexOf("\n\n")` (line 68) never matches CRLF-delimited SSE.** `"\r\n\r\n".indexOf("\n\n") === -1`, so against a CRLF upstream no block is ever emitted until `_flush`: the whole response buffers in memory and arrives in one burst at end-of-stream. Streaming is destroyed and memory is unbounded. `zai-responses-compat.mjs:89-98` handles both separators, and `rewrite()` at line 30 of your own file already checks for `\r\n` — the splitter just didn't get the same treatment.

**3. An unclosed `<think>` swallows the rest of the response.** `#consume` sets `#insideThink = true` and discards everything until `</think>`. If the model opens one in legitimate visible content and never closes it, the entire remainder is dropped — and `_flush` doesn't emit `#pending` either, so a stream ending on a partial tag loses that text too. Note your non-streaming `stripThinking` uses a non-greedy regex that *requires* a close tag and is therefore safe; the streaming machine has no equivalent guard.

**4. `response.completed` is not sanitized.** `rewriteTextFields` recurses into `item`/`part`/`output`/`content` but not `response`. The terminal `{type:"response.completed", response:{output:[…]}}` carries the full unfiltered text, and Codex builds session history from it — so the thinking still leaks into history, and history diverges from what was displayed.

There's also an interaction worth knowing about: in `router.mjs` the transform list puts `EmptyCompletionGuard` **downstream** of this filter. A turn whose visible text is entirely consumed by issue 3 reaches the guard as an empty completion and triggers a retry — a second billed turn on content that wasn't actually empty.

**Separately — `reasoning_split`.** `src/api-forwarder.mjs:792` sends it on every request with `requestProfile: "minimax-m3"`. The scoping is tight (only `config/minimax/token-plan/minimax-m3.json` sets that profile), but I couldn't find documentation or a fixture establishing that it's a real MiniMax parameter. If their OpenAI-compatible endpoint rejects unknown body fields, this 400s every Token Plan turn. The added test asserts the router *sends* it against a mock, which proves nothing about acceptance. Worth a live probe before this lands — and if it works, it fixes the problem at the source and the transform can shrink to a narrow belt-and-braces on `output_text` only.

**On the tests:** the "removes leaked think markup" case splits the payload across two SSE events but keeps `<think>` and `</think>` each intact within one chunk — so it doesn't cover the split-marker path, which is the `#pending` path and the source of issues 3 and 4. Nothing covers `_flush` with pending state, CRLF, a missing close tag, function-call arguments, or `response.completed`.

The state machine is a reasonable sketch and the intent is right. I'd rewrite it against `zai-responses-compat.mjs` — type-dispatched, dual-separator, per-item state — rather than patch these individually. Happy to review again whenever you take it off draft.

Reviewed this while clearing the PR queue. Still a draft, so no action expected — but the conclusion is unusual enough to be worth saying now: **the problem here is scope, not quality.**

`src/compaction-checkpoint.mjs` is the best code I read across this whole queue. It is coherent and defensively written throughout: strict base64, byte-bounded UTF-8-safe truncation, a size-fitting pass with a deterministic drop order, full re-normalization on both encode and decode, secret redaction, and a model-output contract validator that refuses ambiguous embedded JSON. The 27 unit tests plus 2 router integration tests are genuinely adversarial — they assert that reasoning isn't mistaken for the final answer, that an assistant-authored rendered checkpoint isn't trusted, that oversized or ambiguous JSON is rejected, that counters can't produce `Infinity` IDs. That is the opposite of decorative. CHANGELOG and `docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md` are updated too.

What holds it back is that a PR titled "add compaction checkpoints" also rewires the routed request path. Four things, all in `router.mjs`, all on the hot path, all independent of the checkpoint format:

**1. An ordinary turn can silently fire an extra billed LLM call.** `bridgedRoutedHistory` sits on every routed turn (`router.mjs:2628`). When `latestHistoryBoundary` classifies the newest boundary as legacy kcr1 or an opaque OpenAI-native compaction token, it calls the full `summarize()` — vision bridging, agent-payload relay, provider failover — *before* the user's turn is forwarded. So a one-line follow-up in a session that previously compacted natively pays a multi-second summarization against a possibly different provider, with no indication. That needs an opt-out and a log line the operator sees by default.

**2. `historyBridgeKey` does `JSON.stringify(prefixInput)` on the request path** (`router.mjs:1053`), skipped only when a `thread-id` / `session-id` / `session_id` header is present or `boundary.value` is a string. For a message-derived legacy boundary with no thread header, every request re-serializes the entire pre-boundary history — potentially megabytes — to compute a cache key, on the event loop. Worth confirming Codex actually sends one of those headers, because if it doesn't, this path is always taken. (`session_id` with an underscore isn't a conventional header name.)

**3. `rewriteHistoryFromCheckpoint` drops non-user roles.** It discards every input item before the boundary except up to two fingerprint-matched *user* messages — so any `developer`/`system` message, tool definition, or client-injected preamble sitting before the compaction item silently vanishes from routed turns. Top-level `payload.instructions` survives, but a client that puts context in `input[0]` loses it. Needs an explicit carve-out for non-user roles.

**4. `encodeCheckpoint` throws instead of degrading** (`compaction-checkpoint.mjs:455`), called at `router.mjs:1992` with no local guard. `normalizedCheckpoint` can return `undefined` on a bad `recent_tail` id or a missing/invalid `counters` object — and then compaction becomes a 5xx. A failed compaction ends the session, which is exactly what the surrounding comments say must be avoided. Fall back to a minimal valid checkpoint or to kcr1.

Two quieter cross-provider risks worth a look:

- `extractResponseText` now requires `item.type === "message"` (`router.mjs:1651`). Any routed provider whose Responses-shaped output items omit `type` or use a different tag — common in chat-completions→Responses shims — previously contributed text and now contributes nothing. It isn't an error: `finalizeCheckpoint("")` returns a structurally valid checkpoint, so compaction reports `ok: true` while silently producing an empty summary. Pure chat-completions providers are fine (the `choices[0].message.content` fallback is retained); the exposure is Responses-shaped providers with non-standard item types.
- `summarizeWith` spreads the caller's payload (`router.mjs:1699`), so combined with (1) an ordinary turn's `text.format` JSON-schema constraint, `max_output_tokens` and `reasoning` now flow into the bridging summarization. A turn constrained to a user schema would make the checkpoint contract JSON unparseable and degrade silently to the no-model-output path.

**Suggested split.** Land the format work first — encode/decode/render, the kcr1→kcr2 migration, the compaction-path changes — behind its own tests. Hold `bridgedRoutedHistory` for a separate, flagged PR. The checkpoint module would go in on its own merits; it's the router rewiring that needs the extra scrutiny, and bundling them means a reviewer approving "a compaction format" is also approving a change to what every routed turn does.

Three things to fix.

**1. This is now slower than `main` on every credential write, and the comment says the opposite.**

`main` memoizes the SID — `if (windowsSid) return windowsSid` — so it pays one `powershell.exe` cold start *per process* and then runs `icacls.exe` per call. This version spawns `powershell.exe` on **every** call with no memoization, and `powershell.exe -NoProfile` is roughly an order of magnitude more expensive to start than `icacls.exe`.

That matters on a real path: `src/local-download.mjs:305-322` calls `writeLocalDownload` on every distinct `(percent, detail)` tuple, so one model download makes hundreds of synchronous `writePrivateJson` calls — each now blocking the event loop on a PowerShell cold start, mid-stream. `src/service-windows.mjs:143-151` pays two spawns per launcher write.

The header comment frames this as *lowering* spawn count. It does relative to #349's two-per-write design, not relative to `main`. Either restore an `icacls` fast path, re-memoize what can be memoized, or state the tradeoff honestly in the comment. (Also worth noting `protectPrivateFilesWin32` is never called with more than one path anywhere in the tree, so the batching the comment advertises has no user yet.)

**2. A hardening failure can plausibly exit 0, and its diagnostics are discarded.**

`stdio: "ignore"`, and the script has no `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`, no `try/catch`, and no explicit `exit 1`. `execFileSync` only throws on a non-zero exit, and whether PowerShell returns non-zero for an uncaught `SetAccessControl` exception depends on its method-invocation error semantics rather than on anything this script asserts. `icacls.exe` returned documented non-zero codes, so this is strictly less reliable than `main`.

The failure mode is the invisible one: the credential file is written, `writePrivateFile` returns success, and the DACL was never applied. Even when it *is* detected, stderr is thrown away so the error carries no message for a `doctor` report.

Suggest `$ErrorActionPreference='Stop'`, `try { … } catch { [Console]::Error.Write($_); exit 1 }`, and capturing stderr into the thrown error.

**3. `SetOwner`/`SetGroup` narrow the set of DACLs you can repair.**

Persisting the OWNER and GROUP sections requires `WRITE_OWNER`. Windows grants a file's owner implicit `READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC` but **not** `WRITE_OWNER`, whereas `icacls /inheritance:r /grant:r` needed only `WRITE_DAC`. So in exactly the scenario this rewrite exists to fix — a protected but non-canonical DACL that doesn't grant the current user FullControl — `SetAccessControl` can throw `UnauthorizedAccessException` where `main` would have succeeded. Since all sections persist in one call it is all-or-nothing, so the DACL doesn't get fixed either.

`SetGroup($sid)` in particular buys nothing: the POSIX group field isn't consulted by Windows access checks. Suggest dropping both, or persisting the DACL first and treating owner/group as best-effort.

## The UAC path is well built — with one cheap must-fix

I came into this prepared to reject the elevation path and could not construct an attack against its design. The pre-elevation validation is substantive, not decorative: principal SID must equal the current identity, `LogonType` must be `Interactive`, exactly one action, and the action's executable must be byte-equal (after `ExpandEnvironmentVariables` + `GetFullPath`) to this checkout's Tauri or Electron companion. Crucially it is **re-validated on the elevated side** against the pre-elevation values, closing the TOCTOU window. The payload is a single-quoted here-string so no caller data is interpolated into script text, and the blast radius is one `AccessAllowed` ACE on a *Limited*, user-principal task — which does not yield elevation even in the worst case.

**The defect is the launcher itself, not the design.** `codex-router.ps1:175`:

```powershell
Start-Process -FilePath "powershell.exe" -Verb RunAs ...
```

`-Verb` forces `UseShellExecute`, so resolution goes through `ShellExecuteEx`, whose search order includes the **current working directory** and every `PATH` entry. The script does not `Push-Location` first, so the CWD is wherever the user's shell happened to be — plausibly `Downloads`, or an extracted archive. An unprivileged attacker who can drop a `powershell.exe` into the CWD or any user-writable `PATH` entry gets their binary launched **behind the UAC prompt, fully elevated**. That is the classic local-privilege-escalation shape, and I confirmed this is the **only** `-Verb RunAs` in the codebase — so it is the one place it matters.

One line: `Join-Path $env:SystemRoot 'System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe'`, ideally with `-WorkingDirectory $env:SystemRoot`.

**1. `TASK_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 4_000` (2 s per host) contradicts this repo's own precedent for the identical call.** `src/service-windows.mjs:250` uses `TASK_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000` for the same `Get-ScheduledTask … .State` read, and gives `Register-ScheduledTask` **no timeout at all**. The PR also inverts the failure philosophy at the same time: `service-windows.mjs:262-271` deliberately *returns* rather than throwing when no PowerShell can answer, with a comment explaining why; `tray-service-windows.mjs:244` throws. **2. The 4 s cap on `installTask` manufactures the exact state `tray repair` exists to fix.** That one child does CLR start + module load + four CDXML cmdlets + `Register-ScheduledTask` RPC + COM connect + `GetSecurityDescriptor`/`SetSecurityDescriptor`. **3. `deploy-codex-router.ps1:171` breaks on PowerShell 7.4+ on the success path.** `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` at `:9`, then a bare `& robocopy`. From 7.4, `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference` is on by default — and robocopy returns **1** on normal success ("one or more files copied"), so line 171 raises a terminating error and lines 172-173, the entire reason the script knows robocopy's 0-7 convention, are never reached. Needs `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $false` around the call or a `try`/`catch`. (5.1 is unaffected.)

**4. Likely fatal, and I cannot verify it: environment variables probably do not cross the UAC boundary.** `:158-177` passes all four repair parameters via `$env:CODEX_ROUTER_TRAY_REPAIR_*` then elevates with `Start-Process -Verb RunAs`. If that holds, the elevated script binds `-TaskName $null`, fails validation, and `tray repair` has never worked. It **fails safe** — no wrong task gets rewritten — but the headline feature would be dead on arrival, and the only test covering it is a source regex that cannot detect this. ## Why

```js
export function skipServiceManagerCall({ hostManaged = true, env = process.env } = {}) {
  if (serviceManagerDisabled(env)) return true;
  return Boolean(env.NODE_TEST_CONTEXT) && hostManaged;
}
```

On the ubuntu job `HOST_MANAGED` is `process.platform === "linux"` → `true`, and `linuxInstall()` sets `NODE_TEST_CONTEXT: "child-v8"`. So every mutating verb is skipped **regardless of `MODEL_ROUTER_SKIP_SERVICE_MANAGER`** — which is exactly the protection this PR adds. The recorder therefore logs nothing and the control's `deepEqual` cannot hold.

It passes on macOS for the reason the commit message gives: `HOST_MANAGED` is false there, so only the explicit flag suppresses the call. The message reasons about macOS and win32, but not about the module's *own* host, where the skip is unconditional inside a test context by construction. The skip clause only excludes win32:

```js
{ skip: process.platform === "win32" && "the recorder stub needs a POSIX shell" },
```

## Suggested fix

The control cannot be satisfied on linux, so exclude it there as well:

```js
{
  skip:
    (process.platform === "win32" && "the recorder stub needs a POSIX shell")
    || (process.platform === "linux"
      && "on systemd's own host the guard suppresses the call regardless of the flag"),
},
```

Coverage is not lost: the macOS recorder still pins the exact verb list, and the linux-gated test above it still proves the machine's own unit is left alone — which is the claim that actually matters here.

Investigation against current `main` does not justify a zstd code change yet.

`0xC0000409` is a Windows fast-fail status; by itself it does not identify `zstdDecompressSync` (and a process-level fast-fail cannot be caught by the surrounding JavaScript error path). The router already bounds decoded request bodies to 256 MiB.

There is a closer upstream match in nodejs/node#62260: Windows build 26200, a long-lived Node HTTP workload, no JS stack, and the same `0xC0000409`. A later report on that issue says the identical workload did not crash on Node 22.23.2, while this report is on 22.22.2. That is evidence for a Node/V8/runtime path, not proof of the cause here.

Could you please run this controlled sequence?

1. Upgrade from Node 22.22.2 to 22.23.2 or a newer supported Node release, then rerun the router repair/install so the generated scheduled-task wrapper records the new absolute Node executable. Run `model-router codex doctor` afterward.
2. If it still crashes, attach a WER LocalDumps dump (or WinDbg stack), the matching Event Viewer Application entry, and the last router-log lines. A native frame is what can distinguish V8/Maglev, zstd, UCRT, or another dependency.
3. Also attach a sanitized `Export-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Codex Router'` result plus `Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName 'Codex Router'`. Current `main` waits for the wrapper, propagates its nonzero exit through WSH, and registers a one-minute restart interval; failure to restart is therefore a second concrete failure that the task state/XML can diagnose.
4. If possible, capture only the request `Content-Encoding` and compressed/decoded byte counts for the final successful requests, then A/B the same workload without zstd. Do not attach request bodies or credentials.

Thanks for the clarification, and for keeping #497 as the canonical thread.

All four blockers are addressed on the branch:

1. Scoped foreign-state override.
POSIX now exports MODEL_ROUTER_ALLOW_FOREIGN_STATE only after argument parsing and only when --prepare-only is not set, so a prepare-only run meets the ownership guard like any other writer and can no longer rebuild foreign-owned generated state without the transfer being recorded.
Windows is a different story worth noting: CheckoutInstall had no override at all, so a full cross-checkout install was refused at the catalog step and the transfer path the manifest record serves could never run there. It now sets the override only for a full install, in place before the generated state is rebuilt, and restores the caller's environment in the outer finally — a pre-existing value goes back verbatim, an absent one is removed.

2. Bounded restart-counter query.
The readiness guard passes its remaining budget to getServiceRestarts(remainingMs), and the query runs with timeout: min(5s, remainingMs) and killSignal: SIGKILL. A blocked systemctl now costs at most the remaining budget and reads as an inconclusive count; no query is spawned once the budget is spent.

3. Health/restart threshold race removed.
When the counter crosses the crash-loop threshold, the wait gives health one last bounded look (Promise.race against one pollMs tick) before reporting the crash loop. A health answer that settles inside the threshold-crossing query returns healthy; the crash-loop error is only raised once health has had that final chance and stayed unsettled.

4. Regressions added.

Installer assertions: POSIX export guarded on a full install and ordered after --prepare-only parsing (plus a sh -n pass); Windows override set only when -PrepareOnly is off, in place before the catalog step, and restored in the outer finally on both the success and failure paths.
Readiness behavior tests: health winning as the threshold is reached (the exact interleaving that used to throw crash-looping for a healthy router), each counter query receiving a budget inside the wait's own timeout with the wait ending at its deadline, alongside the existing early-verdict, baseline, and inconclusive-count cases.

Reproduction:

1. The service is originally stopped, so the journal records `serviceWasRunning: false`.
2. Rotation swaps to the new caller secret and reaches `secret-swapped`, then the process crashes and releases its locks.
3. An operator starts the service before recovery; it loads the new secret.
4. Recovery acquires the service lock, restores the disk secret and client documents to the old generation, clears the journal, and reports `{ recovered: true, committed: false }`—but performs no service mutation because both stop and restart are conditional only on the historical `journal.serviceWasRunning` flag.

Observed result: `serviceMutations: []`, disk/client generation is old, running service generation is new, and the journal is cleared. The new recovery test covers a contender that starts *during* recovery, but not a service already started in the post-crash window.

The affected branches are `src/caller-key.mjs:206-209` and `:236-244`. Recovery needs to inspect the current service state while holding lifecycle ownership and either stop/restart and verify an already-running service, or fail closed without restoring/clearing. Add a deterministic post-swap crash → pre-recovery start regression.

Tested this route end to end on macOS (Codex CLI 0.154.0, router 0.5.1 at `b90aa60` plus this PR). It fails one of the five live compatibility checks:

```
$ ./bin/test-model 'opencode-go/deepseek-flash' --live --yes
PASS basic response
PASS streaming
PASS tool calling
FAIL stateless tool result: opencode rejected the request for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (opencode Go).
     (HTTP 400: ... [invalid_request_error] The `reasoning_content` in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.)
PASS compaction
```

The same command against `opencode-go/deepseek-v4-flash` passes all five on this host, so it is specific to the new ID rather than to the provider or to the chat wire.

**Cause.** The check replays an assistant `function_call` whose history carries no `reasoning` item. V4.1 Flash is an interleaved-reasoning model: `opencode-go.models.deepseek-flash` in models.dev declares `"interleaved": { "field": "reasoning_content" }`, which the `deepseek-v4-flash` record does not. The upstream therefore refuses an assistant tool-call turn that omits it.

Bypassing the router, both wires reject the same request:

- `POST https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/chat/completions` -> 400 `The reasoning_content in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.`
- `POST https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/responses` -> 400 `The reasoning_text in the thinking mode must be passed back to the API.`

Both need the `x-opencode-session` header, otherwise the edge answers `MissingSessionID` first. So this is the provider's contract, not a defect in the Responses-to-chat translation.

**Why it might still be worth handling.** `carryReasoningThroughInput()` in `src/router.mjs` moves reasoning items from history onto the following assistant turn, so an ordinary Codex turn -- which does store them -- is unaffected. What still fails is a tool-call turn whose history has no reasoning item for that call, which is exactly the shape this compatibility check constructs. #298 added the equivalent handling for V4 Flash and V4 Pro (an empty `reasoning_content` when the history has none); if V4.1 Flash is meant to survive that shape too, the same treatment would need to reach this route.

### Stream runtime
- **The ten-minute stall guard now actually binds.** Before, the router→gateway and forwarder→xAI connection pools used Undici's 300 s body idle default, which is the `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` at ~305 s reported earlier. The gateway's timeout also tied the guard at 600 s. All three hops now derive their limit from the stall bound (`src/grok-stream-timeouts.mjs`), for Grok OAuth only. The stall setting also rejects values too large for a Node timer.
- **Silent Grok streams get a heartbeat.** Codex abandons a stream after 300 s without a parsed SSE data event and then re-sends (re-bills) the whole turn; comments and pings don't reset that timer. While a Grok stream is silent, the router now relays an identity-only `response.in_progress` event (`src/responses-heartbeat.mjs`). It is sent only after `response.created`, only between complete events, and never after a terminal event, as the last pipeline stage. Grok OAuth only.
- **The first terminal event seals an attempt** (the P1 from #652). The forwarder stops reading there, so an upstream that keeps its socket open no longer delays the answer.
- **A failure stated before any content is released at once.** Previously it was held until the prelude limit and then reported a second time. The WebSocket drain after a terminal failure is now bounded.

### Diagnostics
- The routed transport retry and failover candidates now count as observed attempts, and a candidate waiting for headers is attributed to itself.
- When failover finds no taker, activity reports the original route.
- `response.completed` with a failed or incomplete status now settles as `failed` and records `terminalStatus`.
- Native and embeddings disconnects now settle as canceled. A canceled native stream used to be recorded as 200.

### Patch compatibility
- Structured patch paths are refused when a native header trim would change them, including U+0085.
- After #681 made custom tools namespace-aware, codecs attach only to a plain `apply_patch` declared in the request. A raw call under an undeclared namespace is treated as a codec bypass.
- CI now fails a hung job instead of holding the runner: the test job has `timeout-minutes`, and `npm test` has `--test-timeout`. This was the six-hour Windows job on #672.

### Fast
- A routed body keeps `service_tier` only when the route serving it advertises that tier. A Grok 4.6 priority request therefore never reaches a failover candidate or a compaction for another route, while curated models that advertise tiers keep them.

Thanks for digging into this, the symptoms are real and the write-up made them reproducible in reasoning. I traced the mechanism against the libuv and conhost sources and it points to a smaller fix than the one here. Reference implementation on top of current `main`, which you can cherry-pick or use as a diff: `fix/windows-674-consolidation` (commit bb5f6554).

### Mechanism

- Windows Terminal as default terminal ignores `SW_HIDE` (microsoft/terminal#12570, #15311). conhost leaves a console windowless only when the process was created with `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` (`ConsoleConnectionDeservesVisibleWindow` in `src/host/srvinit.cpp`), and descendants that inherit that console stay windowless.
- libuv turns Node's `windowsHide` into `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` only when **no stdio slot is inherited** (`src/win/process.c`). With `stdio: "inherit"` it sets `SW_HIDE` alone, which is why `windowsHide: true` on inherited-stdio spawns changes nothing under Terminal.
- Under the Control Center, `control.mjs` runs inside a GUI-subsystem executable that has no console. Every console child it spawns without `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` allocates a fresh, visible Terminal window. The refresh window comes from `schtasks.exe` queries without `windowsHide` and from the Job Object self-wrap, which inherits stdio. The persistent window is `cmd.exe` started with window style 0 by the VBS.

### What I'd keep from this PR

- `windowsHide: true` on `schtasks` in `service-windows.mjs`.
- The `pythonw.exe` + generated `.pyw` launcher, but with the `.pyw` running `cmd.exe /D /C start-codex-router.cmd` with `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` (so the wrapper stays the single definition of environment, log, and exit code, and the wscript exit-code test keeps passing), and the direct `cmd.exe` form as the fallback when the venv is absent.

### What I'd drop, and why

- Heartbeat trigger removal: regresses #581 (#618, #630). A tick dropped by `IgnoreNew` starts no process, and a tick that relaunches goes through the windowless launcher, so it draws nothing once the flags are right.
- ACL skip under `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`: the helper already spawns with `windowsHide` and non-inherited stdio, so it is already windowless.
- Spawning `Codex Router.exe` directly and skipping the `control.mjs` self-wrap: loses kill-on-close containment. Instead, in `runProcessTree`, when `stdio === "inherit"` on win32 and no standard stream is a TTY, spawn the PowerShell owner with `["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"]`, write the child's output to `process.stdout`/`process.stderr`, and pass `windowsHide` through to the contained command.
- `targetIsActive` pid-file probe: changes presence from installed-or-loaded to running.
- The csc-compiled winexe and `windows-job-host.pyw`: an unsigned exe compiled at install time and a second process host, no longer needed with the above.
- `windowsHide` on `start.mjs` children with inherited stdio: a no-op per the libuv rule; they inherit the windowless console from the launcher.

The router then only needs to bridge messages between that leg and the loopback socket the signed-out session connects to.

## The underlying problem, stated once

The desktop app couples **product entitlement** (may this account press send in the ChatGPT app) with **compute routing** (which model answers). Every symptom we measured traces to that one coupling:

- Signed in + exhausted window → the composer gate locks sends for **every** model, external ones included, even though routed inference touches no OpenAI quota. The gate is fed by the app's own web session; nothing the app-server fetches can move it (verified by serving a synthetic healthy snapshot on `/wham/usage` and blocking the relay refresh — gate unmoved).
- Logged out → the gate disappears entirely (no quota check exists in that mode — verified), but the account-backed surfaces fall with it: usage display, and the remote-control relay that carries **environment discovery** (devbox project folders and run targets vanish from the sidebar; sending to them fails).

So the two modes each amputate something the operator needs. The fix is not to defeat the gate — it is to make logged-out mode whole, by supplying the account-backed data from the router instead of from a signed-in desktop.

## Unified design: router-held OAuth, signed-out Codex, paired relay

1. The **OAuth session lives in the router** (it already stores isolated signed-in account profiles for switching, and already injects native credentials on the relay path).
2. While login-free is active, the router owns `chatgpt_base_url` → loopback (same snapshot/restore pattern as `openai_base_url` today) and serves the backend: synthetic healthy usage, real profiles/plugins/enrollment via stored-credential passthrough. Verified workable end-to-end by the PoC: the signed-out app-server accepted the loopback for the whole HTTP control plane and enrolled against it.
3. Prompts continue to route exactly as login-free routes them today — selected external model, failover chain, local models. No OpenAI inference, no quota.
4. The relay websocket terminates at the router. Two possible upstream legs:
   - **profile-backed**: the official codex client, run from a signed-in isolated profile the router already manages, opens the upstream leg (fingerprint-genuine; a Node client is edge-blocked — verified 403-empty from Cloudflare with fully forwarded headers);
   - **peer-paired**: no upstream at all — a second router install (e.g. on the devbox) pairs over the operator's existing SSH tunnel, and discovery flows router↔router. This fits the common source/sink topology (laptop checks in, VPS does the work) and removes the upstream dependency entirely.

## Why this maps onto existing machinery

- `config-manager.mjs` already snapshots/restores root config keys per mode switch — adding `chatgpt_base_url` to the login-free path is the same pattern as the keys it manages today.
- `api-forwarder.mjs` already reverse-proxies upstream traffic with header rewriting; the backend serving is a new route family, not a new architecture.
- The account-profile store already holds refreshable signed-in credentials; the native relay already demonstrates credential-custody-without-client-auth.
- Fail-closed is the house pattern (native relay fails closed): no usable stored credential → bridge stays down → login-free behaves exactly as today.

## Open risks, honestly

- Whether the desktop UI renders environments whose relay socket is local/paired rather than chatgpt.com-issued — untestable single-ended; needs one two-machine experiment.
- Remote permission-mode behavior once discovery exists (we observed a "Permission mode is unavailable" send failure with no relay at all; root cause unconfirmed).
- Scope of backend endpoints that must be served vs passed through (PoC observed a small, stable set).

I can run the two-machine experiment on my source/sink setup on request; everything above that is measured is marked as such.

I want to be direct about why I'm not suggesting a rebase: as written, merging this would **remove** that subsystem and replace it with one that is weaker in ways that matter.

**Authentication happens after the socket is open.** `acceptWebSocketUpgrade` checks only that `sec-websocket-key` is present, then writes `101 Switching Protocols` unconditionally. `authenticatedRoute(...)` runs later, on the first message. Main authenticates *before* the 101 and rejects with 401.

**It becomes browser-reachable.** There's no `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site` check, and WebSocket isn't subject to CORS — so any page the user visits could complete a handshake against `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/`. Main rejects exactly this with a 403 ("Browser-originated WebSocket requests are not accepted").

**The close handler is a no-op, and the comment is wrong.**
```js
ws.onClose = () => {
  // nothing to clean up; the request pipeline aborts on socket close
};
```
The fake `ServerResponse` defines `response.on = () => response` and `response.once = () => response`, so every listener registration silently does nothing — `pipeline()` can't attach error/close handlers and `stream.finished` cleanup never runs. On an abnormal close the upstream request keeps streaming into a dead socket: a leaked request and burned provider tokens.

Three more in the framing layer: `FrameDecoder.push` parses at most one frame per TCP chunk (two frames in one read deadlocks the second); `fin` is ignored and opcode `0x0` falls through `default: break`, so a fragmented text message is delivered truncated; and the buffer is unbounded (`Buffer.concat` with no cap, `len` up to `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`) on a socket that isn't authenticated yet.

**One thing for whoever touches this area next:** `test/responses-websocket.test.mjs` imports `src/responses-websocket.mjs` directly rather than through `router.mjs`. So resolving the `server.on("upgrade")` conflict in favour of this branch would disconnect the authenticated adapter while all 34 of its tests stayed green. That hunk should not be hand-resolved.

## Fixed in 02eec5f1

**Uninstall could empty the user's configuration file.** Both YAML edits judged a node by `parent.children.size`, which is the lexer's map of keys it was *able to register*. Two things live inside a node without appearing there:

- a block sequence, a merge key, or a key `PLAIN_KEY` declines (`openrouter/free:`)
- a trailing comment block, which `endIndex` deliberately stops before — and publishing inserts *above* it, so the comment ends up inside the block removal then splices away

Reproduced on omp's `models.yml`:

```yaml
providers:
  - name: a
    api: http://a
```

Install produced a document PyYAML cannot parse (`ParserError while parsing a block collection`); uninstall returned `""` and the file was emptied. A `providers:` holding only a comment lost the `providers:` key and left the comment orphaned at the wrong indentation.

`unaccountedLines` now walks the node's indented region instead of trusting `endIndex`. Publishing refuses with the file untouched when that region holds a non-comment line it cannot account for — the same "refuse rather than guess" rule this module already applies to an inline parent and to JSON with comments — and the ancestor collapse stops at anything unaccounted, comments included.

An empty document can still result and that case is correct: the collapse only ever reaches `keyPath[0]`, so emptiness now means the file held nothing but our own block, which is what omp's `models.yml` is.

Added byte-for-byte round-trip assertions — the existing ones match substrings and pass even when bytes we don't own are dropped. Both new tests fail against the previous reader.

Here is the rough Codex conclusion with a quick fix until the pull request is merged / fixed

**Diagnosis**

Every router child goes through `windowsJobProcessInvocation()` in `src/process-tree.mjs`, which wraps the command as `powershell.exe -File src/windows-process-tree.ps1 <base64>`. Decoding those payloads showed that the periodic jobs all carry `"windowsHide": true` **except one**, and that one is the culprit. In this case the tray (`Codex Router.exe --tray-only`) polls `control.mjs chatgpt-account-pool status` every ~60 s and it went out with `"windowsHide": false`.

**Why it happens**

`src/process-tree.mjs` (~line 752):

```js
const effectiveWindowsHide = stdio === "inherit" ? false : windowsHide;
```

The tray's background control operations are spawned with `stdio: "inherit"`, so the caller's `windowsHide: true` gets overridden to `false`. Since the tray is a GUI process with no console, Win32 creates one — and with Windows Terminal as the default terminal app that console gets a visible window.

**Fix**

Only drop the hide flag when the caller really has a console:

```js
const effectiveWindowsHide =
  stdio === "inherit" && (process.stdin.isTTY === true || process.stdout.isTTY === true)
    ? false
    : windowsHide;
```

Now GUI-parented background work stays windowless, while an interactive `control …` invocation from a real terminal still gets its console.

**Verification**

150 s of process tracing afterwards: 8 job payloads, all `windowsHide: true`, and zero new terminal windows. The router kept serving normally.

Thanks for this — the structure is right: the journaled swap is preserved, symlinks are rejected, and leaving hardened-runtime signing to electron-builder instead of a `codesign --deep` re-sign is the correct call. Two things need to change before it can merge.

**1. The release repository defaults to this fork.**

`src/macos-tray-release.mjs:19` and `scripts/download-macos-tray-release.mjs:26` both default to `jiemocoder/codex-router`. Upstream is `duolahypercho/codex-router` (cf. `scripts/update-homebrew-formula.mjs:13`), and `test/macos-tray-release.test.mjs` asserts the fork URL as expected behavior. With the version bumped to 0.5.2 and a `v0.5.2` release already published on the fork, every upstream macOS install would resolve its checksums there.

The surrounding verification doesn't substitute for the right slug:

- `'=anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.1.13] exists'` accepts any Developer ID Application certificate from any team. It needs `and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = "<TEAM_ID>"` in both places it appears (the workflow's notarize step and the downloader).
- `ModelRouterTraySourceFingerprint` is written into `Info.plist` by whoever builds the app, and its expected value is derivable from the public sources. It's sealed by the builder's signature, so it can't be tampered with after signing — but it doesn't attest that the shipped binary came from those sources.

Since clients can't read `MACOS_TEAM_ID`, please export the team identifier as a constant in `src/macos-tray-release.mjs` and have the release job assert `MACOS_TEAM_ID` matches it, so a mismatch fails the release rather than shipping an app every client will reject.

**2. "No package published" and "no network" must stay fallback-eligible.**

`scripts/download-macos-tray-release.mjs:46` throws for any non-200 on SHA256SUMS, and line 43 throws when `curl` itself fails. Only a 404 on the app asset returns `RELEASE_UNAVAILABLE`. Combined with `bin/model-router-tray:368`, that means an unreleased version or an offline machine refuses the local build entirely.

That's the normal state of `main` between tags — after this merges, `v0.5.2` won't exist upstream until it's cut — and it's the permanent state of every branch and dev checkout. The failure is non-fatal to the router (`bin/install` and `src/setup.mjs` catch it), but the companion silently stops installing and updating, and the guidance printed blames a missing Xcode rather than the real cause.

Suggested cut: exit `RELEASE_UNAVAILABLE` for anything that means the package can't be *obtained* — transport failure, 404 on either file, 5xx. Keep the hard refusal for genuine integrity failures: checksum mismatch, a downloaded asset with no `SHA256SUMS` entry, signature or Gatekeeper rejection, metadata/fingerprint mismatch, symlinks, or unexpected archive contents.

**Smaller items**

- `release` now `needs: unified-app-macos`, so a `notarytool submit --wait` failure blocks the Windows and Linux release too. The credentials-absent path is fine, but consider whether a macOS outage should gate the whole release.
- `verifyReleaseMetadata` runs `PlistBuddy` against the extracted bundle before `codesign --verify`. Move signature and Gatekeeper assessment ahead of reading anything out of it.
- `MODEL_ROUTER_PORTABLE_APP=1` drops `ModelRouterSourceRoot` and `router-root` — necessary for a portable build, but it removes the sealed checkout binding that `build-macos-tray-app.sh` documents as deliberate, leaving the Swift host to resolve the checkout from the install manifest or `~/.local/share/codex-router`. Worth calling out in `docs/MACOS-TRAY.md`.
- `CHANGELOG.md` is missing a blank line before the `- **Routed coding clients…**` entry.

Thanks for this — the motivation is reasonable, but CI is red on this revision and I think the approach needs a rethink beyond just getting it green.

### What's failing

`test (ubuntu-latest)`, `test (macos-latest)` and `test (windows-latest)` all fail the same two routed-compaction tests in `test/routing.test.mjs`:

```
✖ router synthesizes routed compaction and safely replays it to native models
    actual: 'reasoning'   expected: 'compaction'
✖ compaction never treats reasoning as final text and falls back to chat content
    actual: undefined     expected: 'checkpoint'
```

Both pass at this PR's parent (`0964eefd`). `npm run check` doesn't cover `routing.test.mjs`, which is why this looked green locally.

### Proximate cause

`shouldSkipRemoteCompactV2` returns `true` when `estimatedTokens === undefined`, but `estimateInputTokens` returns `undefined` for any body under `MIN_ESTIMATED_INPUT_TOKENS` (1,000) — see `src/response-usage.mjs`. So *every small* compaction request is skipped, not just ones under `autoCompact`. The fifth test pins the missing-`autoCompact` case, but nothing pins the small-body case.

### The larger objection

Fixing that branch would move the tests' payloads onto a different path, but I don't think it fixes the design. Codex sends `compaction_trigger` and expects a `compaction` item carrying `encrypted_content` back (`handleRoutedCompaction` in `src/router.mjs`). Stripping the trigger makes the router answer the previous user turn again as an ordinary response, and Codex has nowhere to put that — a genuinely under-budget session would hit the same thing. If the goal is avoiding a lossy summary, I think the router still has to answer *with* a compaction item — perhaps a cheap near-lossless checkpoint, though I haven't checked how well that fits what `summarize` currently does.

One more thing to weigh: the `autoCompact` being compared against is the same number the router advertises to Codex as `auto_compact_token_limit` (`src/catalog.mjs`). Codex triggered on provider-reported token counts, so a byte-ratio estimate disagreeing isn't strong evidence that the request is spurious — and `src/response-usage.mjs` is explicit that erring low costs the turn while erring high only costs a summary.

### Minor

`estimateInputTokens` runs twice on the same body (once inside the helper, once for the log line). Compaction bodies are the largest the router handles, so compute it once and pass the value through.
