Thank you for this report — the detail in it is what made the cause findable, and your workaround is the right one. Apologies for the slow first reply.

**Both of your observations are correct, and they are not in conflict.** `installed:true` was accurate when it was printed, and the `.cmd` really was gone afterwards. The installer deleted it.

## What happened

1. `install.ps1` sets `$ServiceInstalled = $true` **before** it calls `service.mjs install`.
2. `service-windows install` wrote both launchers and registered the "Codex Router" task. That is what `{"installed":true,...}` reports, and it was true.
3. `service.mjs` then waits up to **300 seconds** for the router to answer `/health`. This step lives in `service.mjs`, not in `service-windows.mjs` — which is why the `fetch failed` appears *after* the JSON line rather than before it. You diagnosed that call exactly right: it is a `fetch()` to the router's own health endpoint while the router is not yet answering. The message is bare because the readiness path strips the URL before printing.
4. The router did not answer inside that budget, so the step exited non-zero and `install.ps1` threw `Background-service installation failed.` at line 533 — the line in your trace.
5. The installer's `catch` then ran `node src/service.mjs uninstall`, which deletes the scheduled task **and unlinks both launchers**, `start-codex-router.cmd` among them.

So by the time you looked, the file and the task were both gone — removed by the rollback, seconds after being created correctly. Nothing about your machine, your elevation, or your configuration caused this.

The rollback has a guard meant to prevent exactly this, but it only protects a **reinstall over an already-working router**: it compares against whether a service existed beforehand. On a clean machine there is nothing to compare against, so a first install was torn out regardless — and a first install is precisely when the LiteLLM gateway cold start is slowest.

This also explains why your workaround succeeds where the installer failed: by the time you created the task by hand, the gateway was warm.

## Fix

PR #767 makes `service.mjs` exit **75** when the service is installed and running but health has not answered yet, and both installers leave the service and the client config exactly as installed for that case, printing what to check instead. A crash loop or a dead launcher is still rolled back — those are broken rather than slow.

Separately, #762 (merged) fixes a latent defect found in the same area: `service-windows install` could report a launcher path it had failed to write, swallowing the exception. That is **not** what happened to you — your launcher was written correctly — but it would have produced a similar-looking report with no cause named anywhere.

## In the meantime

Your workaround is sound and nothing here supersedes it. On the current code you can also avoid the rollback entirely by running the service step yourself after the installer:

```powershell
node src/service.mjs install
```

If it reports the health timeout again, the service is installed and starting; `./codex-router.ps1 status` a few minutes later should show it healthy.

One thing I could not determine from here, and would value if you have it: **how long** the install sat before printing `fetch failed`, and whether the router does eventually come up on that machine once the task exists. If it needed materially more than 300 seconds on a cold start, the budget itself is worth revisiting — that would be a second, separate problem from the rollback, and your machine is the only evidence of it so far.

companions. They are the Node runtime.**

## What the chain actually is

Every control command the Control Center runs goes through
`runControl`/`runJson` in `apps/control-center/electron/command-runner.mjs`,
which spawns:

```js
const invocation = process.platform === "win32"
  ? windowsJobProcessInvocation(process.execPath, [entry, ...args], { ... })
  : { command: process.execPath, args: [entry, ...args] };
```

with

```js
...(process.versions.electron ? { ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE: "1" } : {}),
```

So on Windows each command is two processes:

1. `windowsJobProcessInvocation` returns a **PowerShell job owner** —
   `powershell.exe -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
   -File <runner> <payload>`. That is your `powershell (pid 5632) <- Codex
   Router (pid 25260)`, and it is why every one of the six had an identical
   command line.
2. That job owner launches `process.execPath` — which in a packaged build *is*
   `Codex Router.exe` — with `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1`, running
   `src/control.mjs`. That is your `Codex Router (pid 4540) <- powershell (pid
   9988)`.

The packaged Electron binary is the Node runtime. A companion being relaunched
and a control command being run are the same executable name in `Win32_Process`,
which is what makes the sample read as a restart loop.

The two grandchildren confirm it rather than contradicting it:

- `codex.exe app-server` and `grok.cmd --version` are what
  `control providers` / `control account` legitimately do. A **relaunched
  companion** would have created a tray icon and a window; these did neither,
  and you noted the router stayed healthy and unchanged throughout.

## Why six, and why again five minutes later

`refreshAll` in `ipc.mjs` fans out to one control process per section:

```js
snapshot(), runJson(["providers"]), runJson(["account"]),
runJson(["provider-usage"]), runJson(["local-models", "list", "--json"]),
runJson(["vision-bridge", "status"]), runJson(["presence", "status"])
```

— which is your burst of six inside two seconds.

And `App.tsx` polls exactly twice on the same period:

```js
const usageTimer    = window.setInterval(() => void refreshUsage(), 5 * 60_000);
const snapshotTimer = window.setInterval(() => { void refreshCore(); }, 5 * 60_000);
```

Your two samples are **12:59:41** and **13:04:43** — 5m02s apart. That is the
timer, not a retry.

## So what about the unreadable tray state

I believe it was a coincidence rather than a cause. I checked every consumer of
that status document on `main`: the only one is `controlTray` in `ipc.mjs`, and
it branches on `supported`, never on `installed`. The Settings page reads only
`supported` and `why`, and all three tray buttons are manual. Nothing on `main`
turns `state: "unknown"` into an install, a rebuild, or a launch — and
`install-plan.mjs tray-plan` fails closed to `absent` specifically so it cannot.

`{"installed":false, …, "state":"unknown"}` in your `control tray status` is
honest about the scheduler not answering, but `installed:false` sitting next to
it is genuinely easy to misread as "the tray is not installed" — I read it that
way too at first. That is worth a separate look.

## Where that leaves the issue

Both halves are the same defect: **console windows from the per-command job
owners**, which is #775/#744 and is hidden on `main`. There is no second
relaunch-supervision bug behind it, so I am not going to invent a fix for one.

Your workaround also fits this reading: `tray uninstall` stopped the bursts
because it removed the Control Center that was doing the polling — not because
it broke a relaunch cycle.

The minor nit is fixed too: `tray disable` and `tray enable` are accepted by
`codex-router.ps1` as of c41eee53.

**What would be useful from you**, if you are willing: a checkout of `main` (or
the next release) and one more `Win32_Process` sample over ~10 minutes. Two
things settle it —

- no visible `conhost.exe` beside the `powershell.exe` owners, and
- the `Codex Router.exe` children still appearing every five minutes, but with
  no tray icon or window appearing with them.

If you see that, this is closed. If you see a `Codex Router.exe` that is *not*
a child of a job-owner PowerShell, that is the relaunch loop and I want the
sample.

## One thing I do think is worth changing separately

Even windowless, seven processes every five minutes — several of them shelling
out to `grok.cmd --version`, `codex.exe app-server`, and a keychain sweep — is
a lot of background work for a window that may not even be visible. That is a
real cost you identified under Impact, and it is worth its own issue rather
than being folded in here.

For triage context: checked #266 and #505 before filing this — related symptom class (early/repeated compaction from a wrong `autoCompact`/context pairing), but both are different mechanisms. #266 was an *estimate* overshoot on zero-`prompt_tokens` turns against a correctly-small window (fixed by seeding `contextWindow` from the provider's advertised `context_length`). #505 was two fields **statically pinned together** at the old default and never refreshed, since `opencode-go` discovery reports no context length at all to move them off it. This issue is neither: `context_window` for `openrouter/union-alpha` is correctly `262144` (the #266 fix is working), but `auto_compact_token_limit` alone is stale at `131072" -- the two fields desynced from each other rather than both being stuck. Flagging in case it points at a gap the #505 pin-refresh doesn't cover (a live-curated model whose window gets corrected without a matching autoCompact recompute).

These two fields aren't out of sync — they're the reserve rule applied literally, and this pair is pinned by a test. Details, in case it saves a detour:

**Where 131,072 comes from.** `config/openrouter/union-alpha.json:20-21` stores `contextWindow: 262144, autoCompact: 131072` as checked-in data (`compHash: "openrouter-union-alpha-v1"`), and `src/catalog.mjs:669` emits it verbatim (`auto_compact_token_limit: model.autoCompact`) — nothing re-derives it on the way out. The rule is stated for this exact model in `src/union-alpha-compat.mjs:1-3`: "advertises a 262,144-token window and a 131,072-token output. Compact-at-window-minus-output therefore fires at 131,072." A 0.50 ratio is what window-minus-advertised-output gives when the output limit is half the window; it isn't a drift signature.

**The 85–95% neighbourhood isn't evidence of a derivation.** In the shipped tree, 196 entries carry an integer `contextWindow`/`autoCompact` pair. Exactly 6 sit at 0.85 — the value `curatedSizing()` produces (`AUTO_COMPACT_RATIO = 0.85`, `src/curate-models.mjs:117` and `:136-142`) — while 176 sit above it at round numbers and 14 below. If a refresh had corrected the window and left the threshold behind, you'd expect a residue like 0.85 × 262,144 = 222,822. Instead both of your numbers are round and their difference is exactly the advertised output limit, which is the shape of a hand-written reservation, not of a half-updated pair.

**The mechanism you describe has no writer.** Every writer sets both fields in one object: `curatedSizing()` returns `{contextWindow, autoCompact}` together (likewise the default pair at `user-models.mjs:139-140`, and `vertex-support-catalog.mjs:107-108`, `native-context-variants.mjs:34-38`, `local-models.mjs:186-187`, `lmstudio-models.mjs:145-146`). The discovery layer writes the window and never the threshold — `model-catalog-metadata.mjs` (`:94-103`, `:132-140`, `:159-173`) and `model-catalog-cache.mjs:175-195` emit `contextWindow` + `maxOutputTokens` tagged with a `metadataSource` and contain no `autoCompact` at all. Capability metadata and the compaction budget are two layers on purpose, so there is no "window corrected, threshold forgotten" step to point at.

**Where I think you're right.** The invariant you're reaching for exists here — as a test expectation and one documented table, not as a rule:

- `test/registry.test.mjs:849-868` pins `262_144 / 131_072` and then asserts `model.contextWindow - model.autoCompact >= 131_072`.
- `src/opencode-curation.mjs:23-35` encodes the same test for the OpenCode free table, and two entries at `:132-156` spell out the arithmetic ("0.85 ... would leave only 28,500 tokens against the same record's 64,000-token output limit, so declaring 190,000 would let a full-length completion overrun the window the entry just declared").
- The validator itself checks ranges only: `1 <= autoCompact <= contextWindow` (`src/model-registry.mjs:863-869`) and `maxOutputTokens <= contextWindow` (`:870-877`). The reserve relation is never enforced.

So the guard covers two hand-picked slugs and one table; the other ~194 entries have nothing stopping the next pair from declaring an output its threshold doesn't reserve. Promoting it to a validator rule (`contextWindow - autoCompact >= maxOutputTokens` whenever the latter is stored) is the smallest change that would have flagged this class, and the current catalog would still have to pass.

Two things worth knowing while you're in there: the OpenRouter entry doesn't store `maxOutputTokens` at all — its 131,072 output limit lives in the description prose — whereas the sibling route does (`config/opencode/go-messages/union-alpha.json`: `maxOutputTokens: 32768, autoCompact: 180000`), so a field-based invariant has nothing to read on that route today. And `context-window-drift.mjs` already reports this symptom class, but the other direction: it compares observed capacity against the declared *window*, so it structurally cannot see a threshold that is too small relative to a correct window.

Last question, because it decides whether that number is wrong or merely expensive: the Messages route treats the reserve as measured, not advertised — `union-alpha-compat.mjs:6-12` says the hop reserves 32,768 while a request omitting `max_tokens` reserves the whole 131,072, and that entry sits at 180,000 because compact-at-window-minus-output left no room for Console Go's own budget. `clampUnionAlphaCompletion` is gated on `provider === "opencode-go-messages"` (`:20-40`, called at `src/api-forwarder.mjs:1440`), so the OpenRouter route neither clamps the completion nor inherits that decision. If its hop doesn't reserve the advertised output the same way, this entry is holding back 131,072 tokens of room for a budget nothing in that path takes.

Thanks for the response-ID pinning fix in this PR. I applied the Copilot-related commits locally and restarted codex-router.
The response-ID issue is fixed for plain text responses: a simple streamed request now completes successfully with `response.completed`, and the response/in-progress/completed IDs are pinned consistently.
However, tool-calling turns still fail.

## Reproduction after applying this PR

A minimal function-tool request still produces:
invalid_responses_stream: A Responses function call arguments event referenced an unknown item.

LiteLLM then reports:
litellm.MidStreamFallbackError: litellm.APIError: Response API in-stream error


## Raw Copilot stream behavior

For a function call, the upstream stream looks like this:
response.output_item.added item.type = function_call item.id = A item.call_id = CALL_X
response.function_call_arguments.delta item_id = B call_id = absent
response.function_call_arguments.delta item_id = C call_id = absent
response.function_call_arguments.delta item_id = D call_id = absent
response.function_call_arguments.done item_id = E call_id = absent
response.output_item.done item.id = F item.call_id = CALL_X


The `item_id` changes for every function-argument event, while the `call_id` is not included in those events. The final `output_item.done` also uses a different item ID.

## Why the current fix does not cover this

The current Responses adapter records the item ID and call ID from `response.output_item.added`. For function argument events it resolves the item using:

const key = data.call_id || data.item_id;


Since Copilot sends a new `item_id` for every argument delta and does not send `call_id`, the adapter cannot find the previously registered item and emits:

A Responses function call arguments event referenced an unknown item.


## Suggested follow-up

The GitHub Copilot compatibility mode should also canonicalize function-call item IDs, for example:

1. Store the canonical `item.id` and `call_id` by `output_index` when `response.output_item.added` arrives.
2. For Copilot `response.function_call_arguments.delta/done` events, resolve the canonical item by `output_index`.
3. Rewrite the changing `item_id` to the canonical item ID.
4. Normalize `response.output_item.done.item.id` to the original item ID.
5. Keep the strict behavior unchanged for all other providers.

The response-ID pinning fix appears to work correctly for plain text turns. This is a follow-up compatibility issue affecting Copilot tool-call streams.

No credentials, full prompts, or unredacted response/item IDs are included here.

Confirming this on Linux, plus one refinement to the root cause that may matter for the fix: the guard exists, it just misses one spelling of the same thing.

**Environment**

- `main` @ `5e1b49e` (`0.6.0`)
- Linux (headless, systemd user service), Node v24.18.0
- Install path: `./install.sh --target codex --no-tray --providers deepseek`

**Minimal repro**

`config.toml` before install - valid TOML:

```toml
model = "gpt-6-astra"

[features]
multi_agent = true

[features.multi_agent_v2]
enabled = true
wait_agent_enabled = true

[model_providers.some-provider]
name = "example"
base_url = "https://example.invalid/"
wire_api = "responses"
```

With an isolated `CODEX_HOME`:

```sh
CODEX_HOME=$TMP node src/secret.mjs ensure
CODEX_HOME=$TMP node src/config-manager.mjs enable
python3 -c "import tomllib; tomllib.load(open('$TMP/config.toml','rb'))"
```

Result:

```
Cannot declare ('features', 'multi_agent_v2') twice (at line 16, column 25)
```

The managed line lands as a dotted key inside `[features]`:

```toml
[features]
multi_agent = true
# BEGIN codex-router-multi-agent-v2-managed
multi_agent_v2 = { enabled = true, max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 6, ... }
# END codex-router-multi-agent-v2-managed

[features.multi_agent_v2]     # already declared by the user
enabled = true
wait_agent_enabled = true
```

**Root cause: the guard is missing one spelling**

There is a check - `hasModernMultiAgentConfig()` at `src/config-manager.mjs:339`, used as the guard inside `withManagedMultiAgentV2()` (`src/config-manager.mjs:404`, guard on line 406). It recognizes three forms:

| Line | Recognized form |
| --- | --- |
| 341 | `features.multi_agent_v2 = ...` (top-level dotted key) |
| 342 | `[agents.<x>]` |
| 349-351 | `multi_agent_v2 = ...` **inside** the `[features]` table |

What it does not recognize is the standalone sub-table header `[features.multi_agent_v2]` - which is exactly the spelling Codex documents and the one this issue describes as "a completely reasonable thing to have". When only that form is present, the guard returns `false` and the managed block is injected.

So "with no check for whether `features.multi_agent_v2` is already defined elsewhere" is not quite it: the check runs, it just does not know this spelling. If #836 scans the document structurally, this variant looks worth an explicit test case:

```toml
[features]
multi_agent = true
## deliberately no dotted key here
[features.multi_agent_v2]   # <- this case
enabled = true
```

**Impact**

- Codex becomes unusable: the config stops loading and `codex debug models` fails.
- Your own doctor reports it correctly (`FAIL  Codex config loads`), but only after the block has already been written.
- It recurs on every later `install.sh` run / update for as long as the user table keeps this form, so the block's idempotency promise does not hold for this spelling.

**Workaround**

Move the user table into the inline form inside `[features]`; then the check at `src/config-manager.mjs:349-351` matches and the managed block is no longer injected. Lossless, every key is preserved:

```toml
[features]
multi_agent_v2 = { enabled = true, wait_agent_enabled = true, ... }
```

**Separate observation, happy to file on its own if that is preferred**

After `setup` exited 1 here, the run left the host in both broken states at once: the colliding managed block still in `config.toml`, *and* `codex-router.service` still installed and active. The rollback (`trap rollback EXIT HUP INT TERM`, including `service.mjs uninstall` and `config-manager disable`) lives in `bin/install` (`bin/install:355`), but the full `install.sh` path does not call that script - it handles dependencies itself and calls `"$repo_dir/bin/setup"` (`install.sh:366`). On a non-2 exit it only runs `restore_previous_revision "setup failed"` (`install.sh:377`), which resets the git checkout and nothing else. `src/setup.mjs` has no config-disable / service-uninstall path either.

Strict filtering, please — the grouped view is what made me file this.

Reasoning, since it's a real tradeoff: with several providers connected the page is mostly other accounts' numbers. When I've just clicked a provider to say which one I care about, the comparison view is exactly what I don't want, and reordering doesn't reduce the amount on screen at all. This is a "how much am I spending on **this**" question, not a comparison exercise.

What I'd expect when a specific source is selected:

- **Allowance panel:** only that source's cards. No `Selected · <source>` group and no "Other connected accounts" heading — those exist only to manage the leftover rows, and there are no leftover rows if the others are hidden.
- **Usage sources list:** keep every row visible so the picker still works, and keep the `Selected` badge. That badge is the affordance that tells me what the page is scoped to.
- **Everything else that already keys off `source`** (summary, timeline, cached-input card) follows from the same selection.

Selecting the aggregate row (`This router · all providers`, the existing `kind: "aggregate"` entry) should keep today's behaviour — everything, ordered — because that is the "show me all of it" state.

One edge case worth deciding: a connected provider with no measured allowance cards. Under strict filtering the panel goes empty, and I'd rather see "No account meter available" for that source than have the panel quietly fall back to showing other providers' cards.

If you want to preserve the comparison view for others, a toggle is fine, but I'd default it to filter.

   - `SHA256SUMS` comes from the same release as the zip, so it only catches transfer corruption, not tampering.
   - The bundle id and fingerprint are read from the app's own `Info.plist`, which whoever builds the app controls.

   As it stands, anyone who controls the release source, or can set `CODEX_ROUTER_RELEASE_REPOSITORY`, can ship any notarized app.
3. **Tray updates fail hard with no fallback.** Only a 404 on the zip falls back to a local build. The update exits 1 with no fallback when:
   - the release is missing (the `SHA256SUMS` download 404s first),
   - the machine is offline,
   - the checkout's tray sources differ from the tagged release.

   In each case `bin/model-router-tray` then refuses the local build, so dev checkouts and anyone running `main` between releases can't update the tray.
4. **Housekeeping:**
   - `curl` has no `--max-time`.
   - `CHANGELOG.md` is edited directly; please use a `changelog.d/` fragment.

Thanks for the report and the doctor output. Here is the root cause: `mergeNativeCatalogs` in `src/catalog.mjs` keeps every model in the account catalog, then **appends every bundled-only model** from `codex debug models --bundled`. It does that so a stale account cache can't hide models that a newer Codex build ships. For a Free account, though, the bundled-only entries are exactly the models the plan can't use, which is how GPT-6-Sol ends up in your picker.

The fix I have in mind: when a valid account catalog was read, use it as the authoritative model list, and use bundled data only to backfill schema fields. Bundled-only models would be appended only when no account catalog is available. That is already an option in the function (`includeBundledOnly: false`); it just isn't used during capture.

Before changing it, I want to make sure it doesn't hide newly shipped models for paid accounts whose cache is slightly stale. Could you run `codex debug models` (not `--bundled`) with the router disabled and confirm GPT-6-Sol is absent there? That tells us whether Codex's own account list is the right source of truth for your plan.
